Reduced ticket at the municipal swimming pool , the only sports facility still usable . Heat is no longer just a weather event . It is starting to change how ordinary institutions function : schools , workplaces , municipal facilities , health services . <p> My mother is a nurse in a care home . She tells me about days spent rushing from one room to another to set up drips , prevent dehydration and monitor bodies that were already fragile . <p> A friend , in another hospital , told her that some healthcare workers were themselves fainting . <p> Care work is already intense ; in 40 ? C heat , it becomes a physical ordeal too . In these details , a heatwave stops being a colour on a weather map . It becomes a crisis of work , housing , health , childhood and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the shift . France 's public health agency has reported around 1000 excess deaths since June 34 . The increase affects all age groups , but is particularly marked among older people and in deaths at home . <p> Hospitals have seen rising admissions for dehydration , hyperthermia , fainting and worsening heart or respiratory conditions . <p> Across Europe , World Weather Attribution researchers estimate that a heatwave like this would have been virtually impossible at this time of year without human-driven climate change . <p> The comparison with Covid has become almost unavoidable . Not because heat works like a virus , but because the politics of the emergency feel familiar : a massive , known risk , distributed very unequally , still treated as an exceptional episode , with crisis units , individual guidance , overstretched public services , and then a gradual fading from view . <p> During Covid , deaths first shocked , then became numbers . Essential workers were first celebrated , then sent back to their ordinary degraded conditions . <p> Heatwaves follow a similar logic : alert , crisis , provisional @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Nabil Wakim , a journalist at Le Monde newspaper , made the right point after appearing on French public service television . <p> People should be meeting everywhere , he argued , to learn lessons from the heatwave and prepare for the next one ( due to start next week ) : parents ' associations , sports clubs , neighbours , businesses . A heatwave should be treated as a full-scale stress test for society . <p> France is not ignorant . Since 2003 , we have known . I will never forget that summer ; I was 13 . That year , the heatwave caused nearly 15,000 deaths in France and more than 70,000 across Europe . <p> It left a shocking image in the national consciousness : elderly people alone , dying in overheated flats or unprepared institutions . Since then , plans have been created , warning levels introduced , municipal registers set up , prevention messages repeated . <p> France in 2026 is not France in 2003 . Transport , canteens and childcare services all come under pressure . <p> It is not enough to say that everyone is affected . During Covid , we often heard that the virus was " the great equaliser " . Biologically , everyone could be infected . Socially , that equality just did not exist . <p> Not everyone could work from home , isolate , live somewhere with a garden , avoid public transport , access healthcare , or absorb the same loss of income . Covid did not erase inequalities ; it followed them . <p> Heat does the same thing . A professional in an air-conditioned @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ worker on a building site . <p> An older person surrounded by family does not experience the same heat as someone isolated . A shaded , well-ventilated school does not experience the same heat as an old concrete building . <p> Adaptation is often presented as a series of sensible actions : closing the shutters , drinking water , avoiding the hottest hours , calling loved ones , ventilating at night , improving your home where possible . <p> All of this is useful . The question is who is expected to pay the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That forces us back to the central question : what can actually be adapted , and how far can adaptation go ? A classroom or a hospital room can be air-conditioned , but fields , forests , rivers and streets can not . <p> The risk is that public debate finally talks about adaptation while leaving decarbonisation in the background . <p> The longer the transition away from fossil fuels is delayed , the more expensive , unequal and uncertain adaptation becomes . <p> Heatwaves are a much deeper political issue than they first appear . " It reduces the efficiency of everything . " <p> Staffell and colleagues estimate that , in temperatures of 40C , the output of gas-fired power stations drops by roughly 10% versus 20C . <p> The efficiency of solar panels also falls as temperature rises , though Staffell notes that this effect has become less pronounced with newer generations of panels . <p> Even so , the impact of high temperatures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he and his colleagues have analysed and shared with the BBC . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> Over the past week I 've been reminded just how much the future of our communities depends on looking after the things that make this part of Sussex such a special place to live . <p> Whether it 's protecting our coastline , improving our local environment , or securing better services for residents , these are all issues that deserve sustained attention rather than quick headlines . <p> One issue that has rightly received a great deal of local attention is the future of our Coastguard service . Following recent tragic incidents along our coastline -- including off Black Rock in my constituency -- we 've been reminded just how vital our Coastguard volunteers are to keeping people safe . <p> From Peacehaven through Brighton Marina and along the coast towards Worthing , Coastguard Rescue Teams are an indispensable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ weathers , often putting themselves in harm 's way to rescue people in danger and support wider emergency response efforts . <p> This week I attended a meeting in Parliament with Coastguard representatives , campaigners , the GMB trade union ( which represents many coastguards ) and colleagues from across the House to discuss the future of our Coastguard service . I have also taken this up with the Department for Transport to see what more can be done to ensure we protect , reward and recognise the invaluable contribution that Coastguard volunteers make to our communities . <p> Nobody volunteers for financial reward , but we do need to ensure that Coastguards get the support and recognition they need to ensure the future of the service , and to keep on keeping us safe in the sea . <p> Protecting our natural environment also means taking action to confront the nature and climate crises we now face . Last week the government announced the UK 's first Climate Security Taskforce , recognising that climate change is not simply an environmental issue but one that affects our economy , infrastructure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is also heavily investing in clean energy ( including the Rampion II windfarm , which will produce enough energy to power every home in Sussex ) , as well as restoring nature and strengthening the country 's resilience . The climate and nature crises are the greatest existential threat we face , and this government is rightly prioritising this -- but it must be matched by practical action in communities like ours . <p> Here on the south coast we already see the effects of changing weather patterns through coastal erosion , increased flood risk and pressures on biodiversity . Last week 's heatwave -- which placed huge pressure on local services and was especially difficult for vulnerable residents -- was another reminder of why local action matters just as much as national policy . <p> Environmental improvement is n't always about major infrastructure projects . Sometimes it 's about hundreds of practical actions : planting more trees , creating pollinator-friendly spaces , protecting our chalk downland and coastline and making our neighbourhoods cleaner , greener and more resilient . This is something I know many of my constituents -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Downs National Park -- care passionately about , and I 'll keep doing all I can locally and nationally to make sure the climate and nature crises get the attention they deserve . <p> There 's also been some welcome news for Peacehaven this week , with Morrisons publishing revised plans for its long-awaited new supermarket and wider regeneration of the Meridian Centre . Many residents have contacted me over recent years asking when this development would finally move forward , so I know how important this progress will be . <p> I 'm particularly pleased that the updated proposals retain both Peacehaven Library and Community House alongside the new supermarket , while ensuring there 's no new housing on the site . After so many years of delay , we all want to see shovels in the ground at the Meridian Centre , but this is an encouraging step forward and one I 'll continue to follow closely . <p> As your Member of Parliament , I believe politics works best when it focuses on practical improvements that people notice in their daily lives . Whether that 's supporting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ welcoming investment into our communities , these are the issues I 'll continue working on every day . <p> Finally , I hope we all managed to enjoy England 's ( nail-biting ) win against DR Congo on Wednesday . Thankfully , Parliament ended just in time to make kick off , so I was able to enjoy it with my family . The 1am kick off against Mexico on Monday makes it a bit harder to repeat that ( ! ) , but I hope many of you get to see what will be a massive test for us against a very strong home side . @@138668293 <p> SOME years ago , the Church Times published questions and responses concerning the practice of some churches " to disregard the Church of England 's official calendars and lectionaries so as to preach courses of sermons on the minister 's personal choice of readings " . <p> What was of concern for some was the rule to which each of us who is ordained makes a Declaration of Assent -- namely that " in public prayer and administration of the sacraments , I will use only the forms of service which are authorized or allowed by Canon . " These forms of service , according to Canon B1(3) ( ii ) , include any " Table of Lessons " , which , I think , means in the Book of Common Prayer or the 1970s Revised Common Lectionary ( RCL ) , with its three-year cycle based primarily on the Synoptic Gospels . <p> The Canons make provision for some discretion in forms of worship , and Common Worship says that , although on certain specified Sundays , readings shall come from an authorised lectionary , in Ordinary Time @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ after PCC consultation , the minister may occasionally depart from lectionary provision for pastoral reasons , for preaching or teaching . <p> There have been some calls for revision of the RCL while keeping its value in fostering a shared experience across the Christian Churches of reading the same scriptures , which strengthens unity and helps to ensure that the clergy do n't just choose readings that support their own preferences . The Lectionary provides for a broad range of biblical material , focused on the expectation , incarnation , teaching , death and resurrection of Christ , covered across the Church 's year . <p> The Canterbury Earth Justice Lectionary is radically different : a completely new lectionary offering for each Sunday of the year , and some other days , readings from the Old and New Testaments , and Psalms all chosen around one main theme : " Earth Justice in the context of climate emergency ' " . The biblical texts are not printed out , but for each there are provided either anecdotal illustrations or scholarly commentary , with many quotations and references . These are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to understand climate change as an issue of justice within a perspective of God 's love for the earth and all creatures within a sacramental universe . <p> Advertisement <p> This 500-page book is from two American Roman Catholics : Robert E. Shore-Goss , a former Jesuit priest , later university teacher in Missouri , who now refers to himself as an " author and pastor " ; and Sarah J. Melcher , Professor Emeritus of Hebrew Scriptures at Xavier University , Ohio . <p> Their extensive Introduction starts with reflection on the development of lectionaries in Christian worship , and for personal devotional use . They point to the adoption of Revised Common Lectionaries in the 1970s , and refer to Wilda Gafney 's A Women 's Lectionary for the Whole Church , written to focus on women , in reaction to the view that current authorised lectionaries are androcentric . The two authors of The Canterbury Earth Justice Lectionary are primarily motivated by their deep concern for what they rightly call our " climate emergency " , and that , on the whole , the Christian Church has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> They value the " Season of Creation " , now observed liturgically by a number of Churches worldwide . They recognise the global ethical movement of " Earth Justice " , understanding the earth as a living organism , but note our failure too often to hear " the cry of the Earth " . They have set out principles to interpret the Bible in order to promote justice and healing for the earth . This theme is spread across the church year , with groups of Sundays exploring this theme in Advent , Christmas , Wisdom , Lent ( Restorative Justice ) , Easter ( Resilience and Resistance ) , Pentecost , Creation , and Readings in an Age of Extinction . <p> Much of the many pages of comment on the chosen biblical texts is helpful and provocative , but it is not all of the same quality . Sometimes , the choice of text may be queried . For example , there is no reference to Amos or the Letter of St James ; both have pointers to the meaning of justice . <p> I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Some of us preachers need all the help that we can get to engage seriously with the coming climate catastrophe , and to respond in justice to the cry of the earth . I can see that it could be enormously helpful as a resource for congregational study groups , or for personal devotional use . It could well provide a sermon theme for specific occasions . <p> Where I struggle from a Church of England perspective is how this could be consistently used as a lectionary , weekly , presumably in place of the RCL . Would this need a decision by the General Synod ? The logistics of seeking PCC consent and , on occasion , episcopal good will make it difficult to use in our legal , liturgical , and pastoral context . Furthermore , we would lose the positive values of the authorised lectionary : the systematic working through the balance of the scriptures , related primarily to the life and teaching of Jesus , which the RCL -- whatever its shortcomings -- provides . <p> Dr David Atkinson is an honorary assistant bishop in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> To explore the Church Times website fully , please sign in or subscribe . <p> New to us ? @@138669437 <h> Trossachs National Park camping permit public consultation <p> This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today , and has been written by our American colleagues . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park Authority is inviting the public to take part in a consultation on the 10-year review of its camping byelaws . <p> The byelaws which outline the camping restrictions , which were introduced in 2017 , play a significant role in protecting the natural landscape and make it accessible through camping management zones . <p> The zones , which mainly sit along the loch shore , mean that campers require a pre-arranged permit and they regulate fires and firewood collection in the areas . <p> They were introduced after anti-social behaviour , environmental damage and negative impacts on local businesses spiked in these areas . <p> Kenny Auld , head of visitor services at Loch Lomond &amp; The Trossachs National Park Authority , said : " This review marks nearly ten years since the camping management @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for some at the time , but it came out of necessity and reflected our remit as a national park authority to balance public access and enjoyment while protecting the natural environment we all care deeply about . <p> " Our role is to demonstrate that people and nature can thrive together , but that sometimes means making difficult decisions , testing new approaches and being willing to learn from them . <p> " We 're not claiming the byelaws have solved every issue . <p> " Positive progress has been made , but we recognise that some pressures persist . <p> " This review is our opportunity to ensure the byelaws continue to evolve , remaining effective , fair and fit for a changing landscape , a changing climate and changing behaviours . " <p> In the last 10 years , 97% of the 300,000 campers who have camped in the permit zones have done so responsibly and satisfaction scores have remained above 90% . <p> Complaints have also fallen from 324 in 2017 to 40 in 2025 and access has remained inclusive . <p> Commenting on the byelaws @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ member David Fraser said : " My family and I remember the situation here in Balmaha on the banks of Loch Lomond prior to the Byelaws being introduced , and it was dire for all concerned . <p> " Anti-social behaviour , damage to the local landscape and related negative impacts meant that , as a local resident and business owner , something absolutely needed to be done to stop the situation getting completely out of control . <p> " We supported the Byelaws when they were introduced , and ten years on feel they have genuinely made a massive positive difference to locals and visitors from Scotland and further afield . <p> " We continue to support them today but welcome the opportunity for this review to ensure they remain fit for purpose . Organisations like CIF therefore have to find ways of demonstrating the economic value of resilience . <p> " One of the biggest issues in the climate crisis is around crop loss and food system breakdowns , so this can be a great place to invest if there is , say , an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ harvest is not lost in a given year , " Gbadegesin says . He wore the Tour de France yellow jersey for 60 days during his career . <p> Famously , Indurain was an absolute monster on the bike , with freakish physiology : a 7.8-litre lung capacity , an 88ml/kg/min VO2 max , and a 28 bpm resting heart rate . <p> A fabulous time trial rider but considered by many at the time to be too large and heavy ( 1.86m , 76kg ) to be a serious contender in the mountains , he won the Tour de France in 1991 as an outsider before taking the Tour-Giro double in 1992 and 1993 , so he was going for his fourth consecutive Tour de France victory in 1994 . <p> That year 's race saw an Alpe d'Huez finish too -- on the 224.5km Stage 16 . Indurain had already been in the yellow jersey for a week and held a chunky lead of 7:56 minutes over France 's Richard @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he needed to make sure he did n't lose much time in the Alps to his GC rivals -- and we know , of course , that he did n't . <p> Although he finished 12th on Alpe d'Huez , nearly eight minutes down on stage winner Roberto Conti and a couple of minutes behind Marco Pantani -- who went on to finish third in GC -- Indurain lost only 35 seconds to Virenque . <p> There were a couple more mountain stages plus a mountain TT to come , but Indurain looked in control . <p> The previous owner said , " The bike is INTACT , like new and never used by anyone except Miguel Indurain himself . All elements of the bike are original . Everything works perfectly . " <p> Although Jacques Anquetil had ridden an aluminium frame in the Tour as far back as the 1960s and Greg Lemond and Bernard Hinault had ridden Look bikes with carbon-fibre tubes bonded to aluminium lugs in 1986 , Miguel Indurain was the last man to win the Tour de France on a steel bike . <p> Branded @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the late Italian framebuilder Dario Pegoretti , perhaps the most revered steel framebuilder in recent history . <p> Those Dedacciai and Oria tubes are incredibly skinny compared with the carbon-fibre structures we see in the Tour de France today , or even compared with most aluminium frame tubes . The slender appearance is further accentuated by the fact that Indurain required a 59cm frame . <p> Naturally , for a bike of this era , it is equipped with rim brakes and mechanical gears -- the cabling running under the handlebar tape and then externally , unlike today , when even a hint of exposed brake hose seems to be intolerable at the top end . <p> Speaking of the groupset components , Indurain 's bike was fitted with 8-speed Campagnolo Record . Although he had used traditional down tube shifters and non-indexed friction shifters earlier in his career , he was using Campag ErgoPower integrated brake-lever shifting in 1994 . <p> We ca n't say for sure if they 're fitted to this bike , but Indurain was known to ride 180mm cranks ( listed in Campagnolo catalogues but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ leverage the longer cranks provided to push large gears ( when he broke the Hour Record in 1994 , he used 190mm cranks ) . Most pros are on much shorter options these days , and 175mm is the longest that Campagnolo offers in its Super Record 13 groupset . <p> Although threadless systems began to appear in the early 1990s , Indurain 's bike is equipped with a slim-legged fork with a threaded steerer tube connected to a quill stem . Indurain used a 130mm stem . <p> Wheels ? They 're Campagnolo Sigma rims ( made from 7075 Alloy -- T6 ) , and they 're built up with 32 spokes front and rear . Although some brands and pro teams were experimenting with aerodynamic wheels with fewer spokes during this period , for the majority of road stages , riders still used conventional hand-built wheels with around 32 spokes because they were reliable , repairable , and strong enough for mountain stages and rough roads . Vittoria tubular tyres -- just 20 to 22mm wide -- were glued to the rims . <p> Naturally , those wheels @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by Tullio Campagnolo way back in 1927 . Through axles on road bikes were decades away . <p> Clipless pedals were invented even earlier , although Look began producing the first widely used design in 1984 , and most Tour riders had switched from traditional toe clips and straps by the late 1980s . Indurain used Time Equipe clipless pedals . <p> As for the saddle , Indurain used a Selle Italia Turbo like fellow Tour de France winners Bernard Hinault , Greg Lemond and Laurent Fignon before him . Many riders had switched to lighter saddles like the Selle Italia Flite by 1994 . Indurain might occasionally have used the Selle Italia Turbomatic , but he stayed pretty loyal to the 300g+ Turbo through his years of dominance . If it ai n't broke ... <p> We do n't have a reliable weight for Miguel Indurain 's 1994 Tour de France bike but it is variously estimated to have been in the region of 9-10.2kg . You 'll know that the minimum bike weight for UCI-sanctioned racing has been 6.8kg since 2000 , with most bikes hitting the scales @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Oh , one other thing : although Indurain routinely wore aero helmets for time trials , he rode bareheaded or wearing just a cap during standard road stages . The UCI made helmets compulsory during races in 2003 , but allowed riders to discard them during final climbs of at least 5km , before that exception was eliminated in 2005 . <h> Pogacar 's Colnago Y1Rs <p> On to 2026 , and Tadej Pogacar could join the ranks of the five-time Tour de France winners -- the most prestigious club in all of cycling . <p> Pogacar has the option of riding the Colnago V5Rs , but he favours the V1Rs and is likely to ride this model throughout the 2026 race . <p> Colnago launched the Y1Rs towards the end of 2024 and it 's all about aerodynamics . As mentioned above , the UCI introduced the 6.8kg minimum bike weight limit in 2000 , so there 's not a whole lot of point chasing weight improvements beyond that ; it 's far more worthwhile going for an aerodynamic advantage . <p> Colnago says that what it calls its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the seat tube can " follow the shape of the rear wheel and thus be aerodynamically more effective in an area where the cyclist 's turbulent pedalling flows arrive " . <p> The seatpost has to be cut before being positioned . Once inserted , there is space for further adjustment of just 1.5cm . <p> The aim of the ' gull wing ' Y-shaped structure is to reduce the frontal area and allow for cleaner airflow over the main body of the bike . <p> With the Y1Rs , Colnago has taken advantage of changes to UCI rules governing frame design . When it started developing its Y1Rs aero road bike in 2021 , the UCI had just communicated upcoming revisions to its regulations . For a long time , the UCI had a 3:1 rule governing bike design . The rule limited the ratio of a bike tube 's height ( or depth ) to its width at a maximum of 3:1 . That rule was scrapped and bike designers can now go with an 8:1 profile . <p> Filippo Galli , lead engineer on Colnago 's Y1Rs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is 80mm long and 10mm wide since using such extreme profiles would mean increasing the final weight to guarantee the proper lateral stiffness , but almost all of them exceed the former 3:1 rule . <p> " In particular , it would n't have been possible to realise such a thin frontal area , which significantly affects the aerodynamics of the whole bike , without penalising the stiffness of the whole front end ( which is crucial in sprinting ) . " <p> The position of the seatpost on the Y1Rs is unusual , too . It is fixed in place at the point where the top tube and extended seatstays meet . Again , this is now permissible thanks to changes to changes to UCI regulations . <p> " Such a design would n't have been possible before since the seatpost had to be aligned with the seat tube , or at least a straight line should have been drawn along these two elements , " Filippo Galli told us . <p> The tube profiles , the bayonet-style fork with deep legs , bottle cages integrated into the down @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the development of the Y1Rs were aimed at aerodynamic efficiency . <p> Tadej Pogacar won the mountain time trial in the 2025 Tour de France on a stripped-back Colnago Y1Rs and he rode a slightly modified version of that bike elsewhere in the race too . This version was in raw carbon with what Colnago called " a paper-thin clearcoat " to save a little weight . <p> Unlike the stripped-down build used for the time trial , this version came in a full road race configuration with bottle cages , handlebar tape , and 28mm tyres . It also had a 160mm front brake disc , whereas Pogacar used a 140mm rotor in the mountain time trial to shave grams . This is the bike that Pogacar has been racing on in 2026 too . <p> Pogacar uses a Shimano Dura-Ace R9200 groupset with 165mm cranks and additional sprinter buttons on the drops . He uses a Dura-Ace power meter , moving it from frame to frame to make sure the data is consistent . <p> The bottle cages are Elite Leggero Carbon and the saddle is a custom @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bottom bracket is from Bikone , and titanium bolts replace steel wherever possible . <p> Colnago says that a Y1Rs in a typical UAE race build is around 7.2 -- 7.5 kg , compared with a typical V5Rs build that 's around the UCI 's 6.8kg minimum weight . These are a weather event which are becoming more increasingly common as temperatures continue to rise . <p> ? <h> What are tropical nights ? <p> As the UK experiences increasingly warmer summers , the phenomenon of tropical nights is becoming more relevant to both weather forecasting and public health , the Met Office website states . They are identified by consistently warmer nights but also pose health risks . <p> Tropical nights are defined by a night when the temperature does not fall below 20C . Recent studies show that these are not just confined to warmer climates , and that the UK is now seeing more frequent occurrences of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of experiencing three consecutive tropical nights during July has increased significantly due to climate change . In a pre-industrial climate the probability was less than one per cent per year . However , in today 's climate , that probability has risen to approximately 20 per cent per year . <p> Tropical nights can also affect human health , the Met Office explained . This is because the body relies on cooler night time temperatures to regulate core temperature and recover from daytime heat . <p> When overnight temperatures remain high , the recovery process can not be carried out and can lead to increased cardiovascular stress and sleep disturbances . High night time temperatures are also linked to increased mortality , particularly among older adults and those with pre-existing health conditions . <p> At Reach and across our entities we and our partners use information collected through cookies and other identifiers from your device to improve experience on our site , analyse how it is used and to show personalised advertising . @@138739067 <p> The times when overtourism was your biggest worry during a European summer feel like a distant memory now . As 2026 's peak season gets into full swing , you likely have more pressing concerns : Will you get there ? Will you make it back ? We asked industry professionals how to navigate this tricky year of travel . <h> Unfriendly skies <p> The recent Middle East crisis has created instability in the price of aviation fuel . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hovering over European bookings this summer : fuel shortages . " I think the chances of a significant supply crunch have decreased . However , you never say never . What if both sides flips over the table and leave negotiations and we are back to square one ? I 'm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> It 'll take four months after the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to see supplies back to normal , he adds . <p> Although the price of jet fuel has come down from April highs of $122.50 per barrel to $75 when he spoke to CNN last week , it remains high . <p> If you want to have the best possible chance of avoiding disruption , he says it would n't be a bad idea to fly to or through Spain , which has its own operational oil refineries , giving it a buffer that some of its nearby neighbors do n't have . @@138770813 <p> In the ocean 's twilight zone , where the reach of the Sun fades to nothing , the world 's largest migration begins every time night falls . It could also have an outsized effect on our climate . <p> During World War Two sonar technicians made an extraordinary discovery . The pings from their echo sounders reflected off what they thought must be the ocean floor . But the sea was much shallower than they had expected and -- even more puzzlingly -- the seabed seemed to move up and down throughout the day . <p> This was n't the undulating ocean floor , however , but the many inhabitants of the twilight zone making their nightly migration to the surface to feed . This concentrated " deep scattering layer " of marine organisms , suspended in the water column , was so extraordinarily high that it scattered the sound , reflecting the sonar pings as if it was a solid object . <p> Beneath the waves , the twilight zone -- or mesopelagic zone -- starts at a depth of 200m ( 656ft ) , where the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the reach of the Sun 's rays fades rapidly . The last remnants of sunlight vanish completely around 1,000m ( 3,280ft ) . There , the only light is the eerie glint of bioluminescence , produced by creatures that glow in the dark . <p> Every night trillions of zooplankton that inhabit this zone rise from the deep to feed under the cover of darkness . This phenomenon , known as diel vertical migration ( DVM ) , is the largest natural migration of animals on the planet , with an estimated biomass of 10 billion tonnes . As the Earth spins on its axis , diel vertical migration takes place throughout the world 's oceans . " I like to think of it as a Mexican wave , " says Laura Hobbs , lecturer in Arctic Marine Science at the Scottish Association for Marine Science , describing the swell of animals rising and falling , following the night around the globe . <p> Dante Fenolio/ Science Photo Library <p> Bioluminescent lanternfish account for 60% of all deep-sea fish and make up a huge proportion of the deep scattering layer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Zooplankton go to the surface to feed because that 's where the phytoplankton is , " says Hobbs . <p> " Zooplankton " , she explains , is an umbrella term for many different species of tiny animals that live in the ocean . " These critters are just millimetres long , they 're tiny . And they 're swimming hundreds of metres every single day , up and down again . It would be like running multiple marathons . " ( Read about Jailing Cai 's incredible experience of photographing animals of the twilight zone . ) <p> " As the Sun rises , " says Hobbs , " the zooplankton become threatened by visual predators , bigger zooplankton or fish that can see them now in the light . So , they migrate back down into darker waters and stay there to digest . Then they excrete their waste , get hungry again and , as the Sun sets , they come back up for more . " <p> Copley has explored the deep ocean all over the world and the big realisation , he says , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . " We 're told it 's an ocean planet , a blue planet . It treats human labor as a frictionless commodity . The logic is simple : If the number of drivers drops , throw more cash into the pool , and supply will correct itself . <p> The logic is simple : If the number of drivers drops , throw more cash into the pool , and supply will correct itself ( Getty Images ) <p> But there 's a huge catch . Compounding the issue , fresh research shows that drivers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ demanding compensation reforms . <p> A case in point is Massachusetts , where that frustration led to the launch of the first U.S. gig-worker union in May 2026 . It followed a 2024 settlement between the state and rideshare platforms that guaranteed a minimum wage of $34.48 an hour for Lyft and Uber drivers . <p> As business professors who study consumer psychology and supply chains , we analyzed 2 million delivery tasks , completed by over 70,000 drivers for a Fortune 500 retailer from February through April 2022 , to unpack this problem . We discovered that gig workers are n't just driven by money . They 're sophisticated micro-entrepreneurs who perform a strict " mental audit " of every single task to see if it 's worth their time -- before hitting the " accept " button . <p> By understanding these hidden frictions among drivers , platforms can stop overcharging consumers and start designing work that aligns with the drivers ' preferences and makes their jobs more satisfying . <h> The three dimensions of friction <p> Domingo , an Uber driver who declined to give his last @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interview . <p> " It feels like the algorithm is turned against you , " he said . He recalled a night when he had completed 95 of the 96 trips required for a $100 bonus , only to be left waiting 45 minutes in a busy area for his final ride . That led him to believe the platform was intentionally baiting him to stay online . <p> This example underscores why it 's so important to consider the driver 's perspective to understand why traditional cash incentives in surge pricing fail . <p> With inflation squeezing their margins and rideshare platforms demanding a large share of their earnings , a driver 's split-second decision to accept a fare is a high-stakes calculation of business survival . <h> It 's not just the money <p> In effect , drivers consider more than the top-line dollar figure , we discovered . Instead , they evaluate three distinct factors . <p> First is what we call the " efficiency paradox . " Drivers are acutely aware of their pay-per-mile ratio , so they treat their personal vehicles like small corporate fleets @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ logic , if a route is long and inefficient , platforms should simply raise drivers ' pay and pass on the fare hike to the passenger . <p> But it turns out that higher pay alone does n't guarantee that a long , isolated route is worth it for the driver . We found that when compensation rises from $7 to $45 per ride , drivers were only 50% more inclined to accept " inefficient " tasks , such as long distances with few drop-offs . By contrast , their acceptance rate of " efficient " tasks , covering short distances with dense clusters , shot up by 70% . <p> Why did drivers prefer high-density volume over raw mileage premiums ? Because they clear more customers and gain higher earnings , which feels like a win for their microbusiness . To acknowledge this calculation , platforms should group rides and deliveries into tight , localized clusters instead of heavily subsidizing long , isolated routes , in recognition that drivers prioritize route efficiency . <p> The second factor is what we call the " uncertainty tax . " Beyond the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This friction is most visible during complex pickups , such as chaotic airport terminals or massive sports stadiums , where they often have to circle around and around before finding their customer . <p> To drivers , this kind of pickup is a volatile risk that drains time and burns fuel , another hidden tax . <p> Surge pricing tries to incentivize drivers to accept a high-friction pickup . But there 's a better way : Platforms could let passengers opt into " low-friction hubs , " like walking one block away to an easy pull-off zone , in exchange for a lower price . This reduces the cost of uncertainty for rider and driver alike . <p> And last , there 's the " sunset threshold . " The final and most rigid factor is the personal and physical cost of being on the road after dark . Despite the pressure to make money , gig drivers heavily value their safety and personal life above the extra dollar earned . <p> Our research confirms that the desirability of a delivery task drops off sharply at sunset , regardless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an operational drag that money alone has a notoriously hard time overcoming . To address the reluctance , platforms could shift nonurgent evening orders -- say , for groceries -- to the following morning . This approach mitigates the need to offer costly incentives to exhausted drivers working past sunset . <h> What about consumers ? <p> Because algorithmic platforms pass the cost of driver friction directly to the user , consumers hate surge pricing . When you encounter a massive upcharge , the algorithm is n't just telling you that there are too few drivers . It 's telling you that your specific order represents high friction for the available fleet . <p> But consumers can take steps on their own to restructure their orders and minimize the driver 's " mental audit " penalty . <p> One way is to avoid the uncertainty caused by unattended delivery . With measures like selecting the " leave at my door " option or providing clear gate codes , the consumer can reduce the " uncertainty tax " imposed on drivers . When algorithms see these frictions falling away , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ price . <p> Another way is to rethink timing and scheduling , essentially what platforms could do on their side . In particular , consumers should avoid peak sunset and dinner rushes for nonperishable goods . <h> About the authors <p> Christopher S. Instead of placing three separate orders throughout the week from different local spots , for example , they can consolidate purchases into a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ desire for high-density , low-mileage clusters , effectively neutralizing the " efficiency paradox . How you count it has been contested for years . <p> Methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide but disappears within a decade , while CO2 lingers for centuries . Livestock lobbyists argue that a steady herd adds little new warming , and that the usual way of counting overstates its impact . Ireland and New Zealand , two dairy and beef powerhouses , have pushed the case in international fora . <p> The strategy leans their way . Its answer to methane is not a target but a measurement project : emissions counted at farm level in enough detail to reward the farmer who switches feed additives or breeds lower-emitting cattle . The strategy talks of the " biogenic " nature of livestock methane , the idea that gas from a cow 's gut is part of a natural carbon cycle rather than a fossil-fuel emission , which is the lobbyists ' argument . @@138832926 <h> The weirdest things that mess up wi-fi - and how to improve your signal <p> 13 hours ago <p> Thomas Germain <p> BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images <p> ( Credit : BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images ) <p> The world runs on wi-fi , but strange things can stand in its way -- including your lunch . <p> Alex Hills is a pioneer : he was among the first people on Earth to ever battle their wi-fi connection . <p> In 1993 , he led the team that built one of the first large wi-fi networks , as a professor at Carnegie Mellon University in the US . <p> Hills tells the story in his book , wi-fi and the Bad Boys of Radio . But " Bad Boys " is n't a reference to his ragtag bunch of internet cowboys -- it 's the name he gave to the objects and processes that stand in the way of smooth-running wi-fi . <p> Your home may be filled with bad boys of its own , doing everything they can to interrupt your memes . Some such disruptions are unsurprising @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Identifying these hitches might help fix your connection -- and could even change how you think about one of the most important technologies in your life . <h> Microwaves <p> For 17 years , mysterious radio signals baffled astronomers in Australia . Some blamed solar flares . The public suspected aliens . Eventually , they learned the culprit was closer to home : their telescope was picking up bursts of energy from the office microwave at lunchtime . <p> Telescopes are n't the only technology that 's vulnerably to pesky microwaves . They can also mess up your wi-fi . <p> Wi-fi , like most wireless communications technology , transmits information over radio waves . Governments reserve most radio frequencies for specific purposes , like law enforcement , air traffic control and AM and FM radio stations . But some are free for unlicensed public use . <p> For example , 2.4 GHz is one of the most common frequencies used by wi-fi networks and Bluetooth devices . Coincidentally , that 's also the frequency your microwave uses to heat up leftovers . <p> Microwave ovens are shielded @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ if you 've got a beat-up old microwave , or if you open the door before it 's finished cooking , Hills says it can clash with your wi-fi signal . <p> " It 's one of the most significant sources of interference that people talk about , " says Hills . You can get the same problem from frequencies leaking out of fluorescent lights or car ignition systems . <p> " These days , microwaves are less of a problem , " says Hills . They 're built better and wi-fi can operate on 5 GHz instead of 2.4 GHz . But if you 've got an older wi-fi setup or an ageing microwave , defrosting TV dinners can interrupt your memes . <p> Wi-fi and water do n't get along . Among other problems , water molecules can act like tiny magnets that drain the radio signal 's power . If you 've got a fish tank between you and your router , it can create a wi-fi dead zone . <p> Shadowing is the biggest problem people have with wi-fi networks , Hills says -- and not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ through some materials like wood and drywall with relative ease . But if you 've got walls made of dense material like brick or concrete , that 's harder to deal with . <p> " Think of a straight-line path between your router and the device you 're trying to serve , " says Hills . Signal can bounce around a room and find other ways around objects . But the more obstructions you have in the way , the harder it gets . <p> A shorter distance makes things easier for wi-fi too . Putting your router in the middle of the house and getting it as high up as possible are good first steps . <p> If that does n't cut it , you can try using a wi-fi extender , which boosts your signal , or replacing your router with a mesh network that distributes the wi-fi around your space with a series of small devices . That way you do n't have to disturb the poor fish . <p> Keeping Tabs <p> Thomas Germain is a senior technology journalist at the BBC . He writes the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ His work uncovers the hidden systems that run your digital life , and how you can live better inside them . <h> Mirrors <p> Microwaves can interfere with wi-fi signals , aquariums can swallow them up . But there 's another common problem : reflection . <p> Radio is another form of light . And just as light bounces off reflective surfaces like mirrors , so can your wi-fi signal . <p> Any flat , reflective surface like a TV can cause the same problem . You can have the same problem if your walls use sheets of metal in the building materials . <p> If you have a dead spot in your house , picture a line between you and the router and think about whether there 's a mirror or a big TV that might be bouncing the signal away . <p> You might want to consider moving the reflective surfaces around . Or if you do n't want to mess around with your layout , this is another problem that wi-fi extenders can help solve . <h> Winter <p> Rain should n't interrupt your wi-fi , unless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ space . But when the weather gets really bad , things can fall apart . <p> Snowfall can knock out the infrastructure serving a house , neighbourhood or even a whole town -- whether that 's extreme cold damaging the metal inside cables or snow piling up and blocking satellite signals . <p> Heat can cause similar problems . And even if the weather itself is n't causing a problem , networks can slow down when everyone at your house is stuck inside watching YouTube at the same time . <p> It means that disrupted memes may be yet another consequence of climate change . The answer ? Aside from doing your part for the planet , you can pester telecom companies and local officials to take proactive measures . <p> As for Alex Hills , he lives in Alaska these days , where he 's spent a large chunk of his career helping remote towns and villages get online . <p> Satellite internet services have made that project a lot easier , but they pose their own wi-fi " bad boys " . <p> Sometimes , when a blizzard @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ break out the shovel . <p> -- <p> For more insights , sign up to our Tech Decoded newsletter , where Thomas and Lily Jamali break down the biggest stories of the tech world , and help you live a better digital life . @@138868725 <h> British Antarctic Survey confirms Antarctica 's first dinosaur fossil , 40 years on <p> The fossil was collected in December 1985 by geologist Mike Thomson , of the British Antarctic Survey ( BAS ) , during an expedition to James Ross Island , on the Antarctic Peninsula <p> A bone collected in Antarctica four decades ago has been identified as the first dinosaur fossil found on the continent , according to a study published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica . It is a tail vertebra from a titanosaur , the group of long-necked sauropods that includes the largest land animals that ever lived . <p> The fossil was collected in December 1985 by geologist Mike Thomson , of the British Antarctic Survey ( BAS ) , during an expedition to James Ross Island , on the Antarctic Peninsula . At the time , Thomson recorded it in his field notebook as belonging to a large marine reptile , a reasonable interpretation given that the rocks in the area contain abundant fossils of marine organisms , such as ammonites . The piece was stored for decades in the BAS @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by paleontologist Mark Evans , manager of the BAS geological collections , who suspected the bone came from a land dinosaur . ? Believe it or not , this is the first bit of dinosaur ever discovered in Antarctica , ? said Professor Paul Barrett , of London 's Natural History Museum , who led the analysis . Experts identified the vertebra as belonging to the titanosaurs by its distinctive structure , though the fragment does not allow the species to be determined . <p> The specimen was relatively small : it is estimated to have measured between six and seven meters in length , compared with the more than thirty meters of the largest titanosaurs . Researchers can not establish whether it was a juvenile or a smaller adult . The vertebra comes from the Santa Marta Formation and dates to the Late Cretaceous , around 82 million years ago . According to the scientists , the animal died on land and its body was carried by a river to the sea , where it sank among marine sediments . <p> The find provides evidence about conditions in Antarctica @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sheets and was covered by temperate forests in a warm climate . In that period it was part of the supercontinent of Gondwana and remained attached to the southern tip of South America . The authors suggest that the Antarctic Peninsula may have served as a corridor for titanosaurs to move between South America and Zealandia -- the landmass that today includes New Zealand -- a hypothesis that , they caution , will require new fossils to confirm . <p> The researchers note that the retreat of the ice on the Antarctic Peninsula , linked to climate change , is opening access to new sites and could allow future discoveries about the continent 's prehistoric biodiversity.

@@138889648 <h> This 123-year-old air-con system has lessons for managing today 's sweltering heat <p> 14 hours ago <p> Chris Baraniuk <p> Chris Baraniuk <p> ( Credit : Chris Baraniuk ) <p> As climate change roasts cities around the world , air conditioning can be the difference between life and death for vulnerable people -- but it comes with heavy costs . The long history of air conditioning in public spaces shows what is at stake . <p> There is a giant six-blade fan in the brick wall before me . The fan , painted a glossy red and set neatly into a circular hole in the wall , must weigh multiple tonnes . But when I put my hand on one of its blades , it turns easily -- without so much as a squeak , as though it were installed yesterday . The slightest breeze wafts down from the contraption as it slowly decelerates , returning to a halt . <p> " Amazing is n't it , " marvels Alan Luney , senior estates officer at Belfast 's Royal Victoria Hospital in Northern Ireland . " After all these @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , there 's not a noise out of it . " <p> The fan once drew air across a jungle-like arrangement of coconut fibre ropes that were regularly moistened with cool water in the summer . That air then flowed along a 150m-long ( 490ft ) corridor with an upwards-sloping floor . Openings in the corridor 's walls allowed temperature- and humidity-controlled air to reach hospital wards above , through hidden ducts . <p> But to really understand the significance of air conditioning as a health-preserving intervention , you should turn to its historical origins . <p> Chris Baraniuk <p> This original machinery helped keep the hospital cool and its humidity regulated to aid patient recovery ( Credit : Chris Baraniuk ) <p> Although the Royal Victoria Hospital 's giant fan and coconut fibre cooling system has since been superseded by more modern and more hygienic technology , it remains a testament to the life-saving power of air conditioning . Access to air-conditioned buildings drastically reduces the risk of heat-related mortality and one study found that each year , air conditioning averts around 195,000 deaths globally among people older than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ important approach to reduce the health risks of heat -- and often what 's required is air conditioning , or active cooling , " says David Eisenman , a physician and health researcher at the University of California Los Angeles ' Fielding School of Public Health . <p> In hospitals , air conditioning can play a vital role , reducing the risk of patients dying by up to 40% in extreme heatwaves . Hospital cooling equipment failures are treated as " critical incidents " during hot weather . <h> The origins of air conditioning <p> Florence Nightingale , nursing pioneer and social reformer , promoted various hygienic interventions , including the freshening of air in 19th Century hospitals . Most doctors and nurses achieved this at the time simply by opening the windows . <p> The architects of the Royal Victoria Hospital 's wards in 1903 sought to create a healthy environment in a city where infant mortality was high and pollution from factories and mills was diabolical . The water-soaked coconut ropes not only cooled incoming air , they captured soot and dust , too . <p> " It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " says Nigel Keery , head of estates operations at the Belfast Health and Social Care Trust . " That involved not having to open windows where coal dust and soot was coming in . " <p> The resulting system -- parts of which were made by the same company that manufactured ventilation fans for the Titanic -- was " very effective " , he adds . Doctors working at the hospital reported outdoor temperatures of 26C ( 80F ) in the shade during the summer after the facility opened to patients . But the air conditioning system kept the wards inside to a far more comfortable 18C . <p> Hospital designers and medical professionals of the early 20th Century had clearly recognised the benefits of indoor air control as health-boosting . Gradually , people began to promote such interventions in other places . <h> Cooling stations for overheated cities <p> Today , in the Indian city of Jodhpur , there is a public cooling station -- a cabin-like building that , for the past two years , has offered relief to people during periods of extreme heat . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ around 50C ( 122F ) . To combat this , the cabin 's walls are partly made of fibrous panels made from a dried grass called khus that is misted with water . It 's a traditional way of cooling indoor spaces -- and very much like the moistened coconut ropes in the Royal Victoria Hospital . <p> Electric fans powered by solar energy pull air across the damp khus curtains at the Jodhpur cooling station , lowering the temperature inside by as much as 12C ( 22F ) . <p> " It has been actively used since it was inaugurated in 2024 , " says Prima Madan , director of cooling and climate resilience at the Natural Resources Defense Council , a non-profit advocacy group that was involved in the cooling station 's design . The facility is frequently used by people who spend significant time outdoors including women , delivery drivers and street vendors . <p> This concept of providing publicly accessible cool spaces fitted with air conditioners is catching on . Spain recently announced a national programme to establish a network of climate shelters -- air-conditioned spaces @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sit . <p> " If you know that five minutes from your house or your workplace , or on the way from the market , you start to feel too hot but you can reach a climate shelter within 100m ( 328ft ) -- I think that 's essential , " says Ana Terra Amorim-Maia , a climate adaptation scientist at the Basque Centre for Climate Change in Spain , who has studied climate shelters in the country . <h> Maps for cooler spaces <p> Cities that have previously not had to worry much about high temperatures are also now turning to public cooling in order to help citizens cope . Officials in the city of London have launched an interactive map identifying libraries , museums , concert venues and other locations that are reliably cool . Churches , which are often naturally cool during hot weather due to their stone construction , are also listed . <p> Some people are seeking their own answers to the question , " Where can I cool down ? " <p> One London resident , Tianyin Pan , recently made an online map @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have , air conditioning . He created Stay Cool , an online directory of restaurants , pubs and caf ? s compiled using publicly available data on , for example , building energy performance . Pan cautions that the website is not 100% accurate but says he is working to update and improve it . <p> Public access to cool spaces is only going to become more sought-after as global temperatures rise , says Niamh O Regan , senior researcher at the Social Market Foundation , a think tank based in the UK . " I think people have n't maybe adjusted to the fact that this will become much more normal . " <p> Getty Images <p> The 2003 heatwave in France was deadly , and many hospitals were not well equipped to stay cool ( Credit : Getty Images ) <h> Learning from past disasters <p> To see just how disastrous extreme heat can be for human health and the difference air conditioning can make , the devastating heatwave that struck Europe in 2003 offers a stark example . It killed more than 20,000 people -- some of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pital Saint-Joseph in Paris , where intensive care doctor Beno ? t Misset worked at the time . <p> " I remember very well the heatwave of 2003 , " says Misset , who is now retired . A young postman , whose car lacked air conditioning . The temperature inside the vehicle must have reached 50C ( 122F ) or more , estimates Misset . " He got out of the car and collapsed in the street . He was transferred to the hospital -- and he died . " <p> Misset and his colleagues were also struggling in the sweltering conditions . " <h> The environmental cost <p> Despite his experience , and the study 's results , Misset remains somewhat cautious about air conditioning because of its environmental impact , along with the cost of installing and running it . <p> Coconut fibre ropes used to be wetted to pass cool , moist air to hospital wards in Belfast 's Royal Victoria Hospital ( Credit : Chris Baraniuk ) <p> However , alternatives such as passive cooling -- achieved by shading buildings and windows , painting roofs white to reflect heat or adding insulation to block heat from getting inside -- may not be enough in many places , says Catherine Noakes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the UK . <p> " We 've gone past being able to do it all passively , particularly in cities , " she says . " <p> There is huge demand from hospitals around the world for air conditioning systems at the moment , says Jose La Loggia , EMEA group president at Trane Technologies , which has many clients in the healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors . 
@@138891593 <h> The heatwave that summer was monstrous <p> It 's the summer of 1976 , and on the front of the local paper there 's a picture of a skeleton sitting on the parched earth where the waters of Devon 's Fernworthy reservoir used to lap . <p> The skeleton 's parasol gives scant protection from the scorching heat and its fishing tackle has n't seen the water for a very long time . <p> The picture by Express and Echo photographer John Ffoulkes became one of the iconic images of the Great Drought which gripped Britain exactly 50 years ago . <p> The burning question is , as climate change raises temperatures around the world , are we in for another one ? <p> The summer of 76 was one of the driest and hottest on record . There were severe water shortages across parts of the West Country , with temperatures staying over 30C for long spells and river and reservoir levels falling . <p> No rain fell on South Devon for 45 days through July and August . The previous summer had also been unusually dry , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were told to cut their water use . Hosepipes were banned and households were told to share bath water , then use it to water their plants after they had got out of it . <p> The South West Water Authority - the nationalised fore-runner of the privately-owned South West Water of today - responded by installing standpipes on many street corners . Domestic taps were shut off to conserve dwindling supplies and households had to go out and queue with their neighbours to fill buckets . <p> At Barton in Torquay engineers drilled down to create a bore hole into a long-forgotten underground spring . <p> There was a similar ' window ' when businesses in parts of Scotland closed down for the last two weeks in July , releasing their workers to go in search of fun in the sun during what became known as Glasgow Fortnight . <p> South Devon 's railway stations were thronged with new arrivals every Saturday morning , with big diesel engines bringing trains from the Midlands , the North , London and Scotland every few minutes . <p> The coach stations also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Royal Blue and Grey Cars bringing more new visitors to enjoy the many events on the summer calendar . <p> In Torbay , each train and coach would be met by minibuses from the holiday camps which ringed the English Riviera . At one time Fred Pontin 's leisure empire ran three large camps in Torbay - one each in Paignton , Torquay and Brixham . <p> Traveling to Devon by road was much tougher in 1976 , and not just because cars of the day were more likely to expire in a cloud of steam than those of today . <p> The M5 motorway to its most southerly point at Exeter would not be fully completed until 1977 . @@138912413 <h> What is the best clothing to keep you cool in a heatwave ? <p> 3 August 2023 <p> Lucy Sherriff <p> Getty Images <p> Is it dry or humid ? This is the ultimate question when choosing what to wear . <p> As the world continues to grapple with extreme heatwaves , which are becoming ever more regular thanks to climate change , the clothing we wear is a vital component in how we stay cool . Researchers have found that by wearing appropriate clothes , it is possible to turn the air-conditioning up by 2C ( 3.6F ) -- which over the long term would save considerable energy , both saving money and cutting greenhouse gas emissions . <p> So what should you wear to stay cool ? <p> Colour and design <p> When it comes to colour , most people wear white in the summer -- because white reflects the sun 's rays , rather than absorbing the light like black does . <p> However , this theory gets a little more complex when we start talking about the thickness and fit of clothing , because heat @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from our bodies too . When that heat from our bodies hits the white clothing , it is reflected back at us . <p> In 1980 , a study of why Bedouins -- an indigenous , semi-nomadic people who inhabit desert regions in the Arabian peninsula , Middle East and North Africa -- wear black robes in the desert , found that heat exposure was the same whether tribal members wore black or white robes . <p> Getty Images <p> It 's not always possible to wear the most suitable clothing for hot conditions , but a damp scarf around the head or neck can help ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> How is that possible ? <p> Black coloured fabrics are a better radiator of heat -- meaning they absorb heat emanating from the body -- so this can also play a role in cooling your body down . The Bedouin 's secret is wearing loose-fitting black clothing , especially if it 's windy . The loose black clothes heat up the space between the fabric and the skin , promoting an upward air current -- like a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ amount of heat gained by a Bedouin exposed to the hot desert is the same whether he wears a black or a white robe , " the study notes . " The additional heat absorbed by the black robe was lost before it reached the skin , " it says . <p> So the fit of the clothing is actually more important than the colour . However , if you are going to be wearing tight-fitting clothing , then stick with white . Fabrics with texture -- such as seersucker or pique , a fabric often used in sports polo shirts -- also help to lift clothing off your skin , rather than staying snug and tight-fitting . <p> In terms of clothes , it 's better to have a material that allows water vapour to pass through so that it does n't block the sweat evaporation -- Rhett Allain <p> Material matters <p> " Your choice of fabric is crucial , " says stylist and fashion writer Heather Newberger . " If you 're wearing an oversized denim jumpsuit - you 're going to feel way hotter than your @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ chiffon . " <p> When it comes to fit , lightweight woven fabrics such as cotton and silk are usually better at hanging loosely than knits . This is especially important when it 's humid -- in dry heat , wicking alone may be enough because the sweat will be absorbed from your body and evaporate in the heat . When it 's humid and hot , the air around you is already saturated with water vapour , meaning the sweat your clothes just soaked up does n't have anywhere to go . <p> " In terms of clothes , it 's better to have a material that allows water vapour to pass through so that it does n't block the sweat evaporation . " says Rhett Allain , associate professor of physics at Southeastern Louisiana University . " Some of the newer sports-based materials do this . Cotton does not do so great with this . " <p> All textiles trap infrared radiation given off by the body to some degree , which helps to keep us warm in cold weather -- but is n't ideal on a hot @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cotton , linen , nylon and polyester are all classed as breathable fabrics to some degree -- meaning they allow sweat and heat to escape through the material . They 're different to wicking fabrics , though , which actively pull water from your body . <p> Cotton and polyester absorb and reflect the majority of the infrared that hits them -- nearly 99% -- meaning they often appaer white in infrared images . But these materials also allow 30-40% of visible light through . This combination can cause the body to warm up faster than it otherwise would , according to researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology ( MIT ) . This occurs because the incoming visible light can generate heat that can then not escape as infrared radiation generated by the body . <p> But the body 's other cooling mechanism -- sweating -- also plays a role . Cotton absorbs moisture but it does n't dry quickly , so if you 're sweating a lot your clothes will stay wet , making them less comfortable . Linen is widely worn as it has excellent breathability due @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ slow to dry . Merino wool has been a popular choice for outdoor enthusiasts as it 's breathable and wicks moisture without retaining odour . <p> Another group experimented with garments laced with strips that flatten and bend to help cool the body down by more than 2C ( 3.6F ) . In hot weather , the strips bend towards the air , dissipating heat from the body . Other teams have been exploring " phase-change " materials that incorporate capsules or fibres of material that melt as they warm up , helping to absorb excess heat . <p> Getting wet <p> Perhaps , the best way to stay cool in the heat when it comes to clothing is actually just wearing wet clothes , Allain points out . Water needs heat energy to evaporate , and as it makes this transition from a liquid to a gas , it uses the heat coming from your body , cooling your skin and lowering your body temperature . <p> So it turns out that picking an outfit to stay cool is a little more complex than simply throwing on a white @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ occasionally a splash of water when possible should help you keep your temperature down when the mercury heats up -- and save on air-conditioning too .

Researchers also think they would have played a key role in the beginning of life . <p> But despite that importance , astronomers still do not know how those sugars could have formed , here or elsewhere . Experiments in laboratories , for instance , show that they would not form in the conditions that were around before life was . <p> Astronomers have previously found sugars on samples from meteorite and asteroids , suggesting that some of them might have come from the primordial molecular cloud that formed our solar system . But no samples had been found in the interstellar medium that sits between @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ such a sample towards the molecular cloud known as G+0.693-0.027 , which is near the middle of our Milky Way galaxy . <p> They spotted it using the ultra-sensitive surveys powered by two powerful telescopes . <p> In data from those telescopes , researchers found data that matched erythrulose when it is measured in a laboratory . <p> That research also showed that the complex sugar -- which is the only possible four-carbon ketone -- is vastly more common than similar , less complex three-carbon sugars , of which they found none . " This finding was unexpected , as the prevailing view in astrochemistry is that interstellar molecules grow in size through the sequential addition of carbon atoms " , said Izaskun Jimenez Serra , the lead author on the new work . <p> That suggests that the some 0.5 and 50 million tonnes of the sugar could have arrived on Earth during the Late Heavy Bombardment , about 4 billion years ago . In doing so , it might have helped start the development of life on Earth , the researchers said . <p> The work is published @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ four-carbon sugar in interstellar space ' , published in the journal Nature Astronomy . <h> Join our commenting forum <p> Join thought-provoking conversations , follow other Independent readers and see their replies

@@138948342 <p> As Michael Cloud Duguay points out , church organs are the only instruments that form part of a building . Organs only play in the place where they were constructed , and people come to them if they want to listen . Duguay is a composer and producer from Ontario , and he describes Kingdom Come , Kingdom Go as " almost " a documentary about organs . Using recordings made during a nine-day road trip around the remote fringes of Newfoundland , the album is built around the sounds of organs in seven different churches -- in places called things like Agathuna , Bonavista and Cupids . <p> Kingdom Come , Kingdom Go is a complex , multi-layered album with a strong documentary flavour -- not only bringing these crumbling instruments to life , but exploring the places they belong to . The music they play features , but so do the sounds of creaking bellows , wooden clunking and shifting , and the wind whistling through bell towers . Tracks also feature the recorded voices of people who live on the Newfoundland coast , discussing church attendance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ much part of the music as the organs themselves . And each instrument has been sampled , becoming an electronic resource for musicians and composers . <p> There is another element to the project : climate change . Church organs are highly sensitive to temperature and humidity , and are therefore witnesses to the weather . Researchers have realised that the tuning logs kept over centuries are , in fact , a record of how conditions have altered . The album is a record of sound in particular conditions , which may not exist in future . Whether they will remain playable at all is uncertain . <p> The conceptual richness of Cloud Duguay 's project is matched by its musical depth . The album is unpredictable and enthralling . ' River of Ponds ' , for example , combines wheezing bellows with resonant chords , a spectral choir and the muttered atmosphere of pre-service conversation . ' Winterhouse ' features an ululating female vocal over a repeating organ figure . Strings appear on ' Little Seldom " , dancing while a gruff male voice discusses human nature . ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ drone throughout . ' Pond 3 ' , the final track , is a hymn tune performed by a 90-year old church organist . <p> Kingdom Come , Kingdom Go is a rich and absorbing work . The evocative organ sounds can not be separate from a particular time , place and mood , and are a musical representation of a culture threatened on all slides . But its decay brings forth new life , as Cloud Duguay shows off the power of the instruments he has tracked down , allowing them to slip their leases and perform as though they are expressing themselves without constraint . A far-off , mysterious world comes to life through the speakers .

@@138968289 <p> It 's not difficult to accidentally learn too much about bugs.Unfortunately , though , we have to , because they 're spreading out , inventing new ways to torture us and just generally making life less pleasant . <p> Take houseflies : They thrive in warmer temperatures , and it turns out they 're not just annoying ; they can also be what bug nerds call mechanical vectors of disease . Put simply , it means they walk through garbage and then around your countertops , leaving salmonella and untold other pathogens along with their tiny fly footprints . <p> Or how about longhorned ticks ? They first popped up on American shores in 2017 -- and they can clone themselves . Female ticks just make thousands of self-Xeroxes ; on the extremely rare occasions males are produced , it 's thought to be by mistake . @@138973320 <p> Baby boomers , the generation born between 1946 and 1964 , get a lot of flak from younger generations . The argument goes that boomers had every advantage younger people do n't and likely wo n't when they are older : cheap housing , free university , jobs for life , lower cost of living , triple-locked pensions , and so on . Boomers are the wealthiest generation ever to have lived -- and , younger people contend , they got that wealth simply by being born at the right time . <p> But , boomers point to huge shifts which happened as they grew up that suggest the opposite -- the volatility of the 70s , deindustrialisation , unemployment , the threat of nuclear war -- and say that young people who followed them have had more choices available to them at every stage of their lives . <p> Apart from " I know you are , but what am I ? " -- which I trust most of us left at primary school -- was there ever a catchphrase more witless than " OK boomer " ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ viral in 2019 when the 25-year-old New Zealand MP Chloe Swarbrick used it to silence an opposing colleague who heckled her during a lecture about climate change . <p> It 's thankfully fading now -- maybe millennials finally realised how thick it made them sound -- but for a few years you could n't get away from it . Any time anyone born between 1946 and 1964 pointed out that the world possibly was n't in the worst shape ever , there it was , that blank excuse for a comeback : " OK boomer " . <p> The subtext was clear . We were the luckiest generation ever , so we had no right to comment on what torment the young generation were living through , what with global warming and the avocado shortage . <p> I 've always liked being a reviled outsider , so I quickly took to the boomer label and wore it with pride . Besides , I know that boomers were n't especially lucky ; we were simply prepared to work hard for what we wanted and never expected someone to come knocking on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on an ethically-sourced silver platter . Wartime rationing did n't end until 1954 , so my older fellow boomers grew up basically not knowing what a banana was ; it was n't exactly a non-stop riot of fun and games when I was a child in the 60s and early 70s either . <p> The shops were closed on Sunday ( everything was closed on Sundays except the churches and Sunday schools ) and also on one afternoon during the week , a situation which was n't fully altered until the Sunday Trading Act of 1994 . Of course there was no Amazon , so if your household ran out of toilet paper on a Saturday evening , you 'd be looking resignedly at that discarded Sunday paper till Monday morning mercifully dawned . <p> There was no distracting yourself from your toilet travails with a box-set , because there were n't any streaming channels . As a very young child I recall two television channels , BBC and ITV ( only an hour of children 's TV a day -- none of your CBeebies nonsense ) and then the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was added in 1982 , the newspapers got so over-excited that there was nothing but the new TV channel in the actual headlines for ages . " CHANNEL BORE ! " one paper would blare ; " CHANNEL SWORE ! " their rival would tut . <p> For quite a few years , even watching this outlandish channel with its outrageous programmes like Brookside ( a soap set in Liverpool ) and Hollyoaks ( a soap set in Chester ) made one feel a bit of an outlaw ; that there would come a day when hundreds of channels would be available would have made our heads explode . <p> What were the brightest minds of the boomer generation doing instead ? We were being bored . This in turn often made us determined to get out of the neighbourhood we had been born into , whether by joining the army or running off to London to be a writer , as I did at the age of 17 in 1976 . I considered myself the luckiest girl in the world to get my dream job -- working for a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vote . But , my word , I had a rude awakening when I left my affluent working-class home and had to make my own way . I was paid so little that in order to afford the bus to work , I would ferret through rubbish bins to find glass bottles which could be returned to a corner shop for a few pennies . <p> Of course , I can see why youngsters feel sorry for themselves . I 'd hate to be young today . Nepotism has placed its dead hand on not just the establishment professions like politics , but has taken over the raffish " glamour " professions ; in my day , no posh person wanted their spawn to be a model or a journalist . Social media and the rise of the influencers means that the rest of their cohort see people rewarded for simply BEING . This may well make working for a living seem unappealing . Still , it would seem advisable to take any job rather than have no job . This is the unhappiest generation on record , and having @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ situation . <p> Because if you do n't fight for what you want , and just give up and let life wash over you , you 're basically waiting to die -- what a waste ! Not me ; I 'll keep buggering on till the end . I 've worked since I was legally still a child -- paying tax from the start -- and I 'm working and paying tax still , half a century later , as an OAP .
