@@139000365 <h> This Greek island has a dark past . Now it 's covered in rare seals <p> For half a century , Gyaros was off-limits to the world as a military prison and naval firing range . Then came an astonishing photograph . <p> The Sun is already high above the speedboat when Gyaros appears on the horizon , a desolate silhouette in the Aegean Sea . <p> As we draw closer , a hulking structure of red brick comes into view -- the prison which gave the island the moniker " Devil Island " . <p> We 've journeyed just half an hour from Syros , the administrative heart of the Cycladic islands , southeast of mainland Greece . Sail in any direction and you 'll find quintessentially Greek islands like Mykonos or Andros -- whitewashed houses scattered on hillsides like sugar cubes tipped from a bowl , ferries arriving on schedule , tavernas open . <p> Gyaros never got that memo . It offers only scree and scrub , appearing empty , lifeless even . But it is not . <p> The reason is rooted in a particularly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ authoritarian regime followed by military training left this island untouched by development , a forgotten relic of a turbulent past . Then , in 2004 , an unexpected photograph focussed attention on this apparently desolate place once more , but for very different reasons . <p> Devil Island , it turned out , had become a wildlife haven , offering a sanctuary for a rare seal which was , at the time , threatened with extinction . <h> ' Devil Island ' <p> Isolation , violence and punishment long defined Gyaros , which was used to exile political prisoners as far back as Roman times . Its most brutal chapter , though , began in 1948 , when the Greek state expropriated the property of its last 31 residents and turned it into a prison island . <p> In the initial wave during the late 1940s , following the end of the Greek Civil War , prisoners were forced to live in tents through sweltering summers and freezing winters , labouring to build the brick walls of the prison . <p> After a pause , a second wave of imprisonment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from 1967 to 1974 . Officially a reformatory , where dissidents would be turned into " real Greeks " , Gyaros was in reality a place of forced labour and torture , tucked far away from critical eyes . <p> After the junta fell in 1974 , the navy used the island as a bombing range until 2002 . It still has no hotels , ferry connections or residents . <h> Seal hideaway <p> After the navy stopped its activities , fishermen began reporting sightings of Mediterranean monk seal around the island . <p> Then came a photograph . Taken by an amateur speargun fisherman in the early 2000s , it showed a monk seal mother and pup lounging on an open beach in broad daylight -- a scene that had all but disappeared from the Mediterranean . <p> " Personally , I had never seen it in Greece , " says biologist Panos Dendrinos of the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Monk Seal , an Athens-based research group . " It looked like an ancient picture . " <p> MOm <p> Taken by a speargun @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on Gyaros spearheaded the start of systematic research on the island ( Credit : MOm ) <p> Once a common species , by the late 20th Century , the global population of Mediterranean monk seals had collapsed to just 350-450 individuals . Hunted for centuries for their fur , meat and blubber , coastal development also destroyed their habitat , while fishermen would kill them in retaliation for raiding their nets . <p> The fisherman 's image prompted the first scientific expeditions to Gyaros , where a substantial colony of around 70 adult seals was found -- possibly the largest in the Mediterranean at the time . But it was the animals ' behaviour -- seals nursing their young on open beaches -- that truly stunned the experts . <p> " That was their natural behaviour , " says Spyros Kotomatas , biologist and senior marine conservation officer at WWF Greece , who worked for the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Monk Seal at the time . " Seals elsewhere behaved like Greeks in Athens -- tense , alert . On Gyaros , they were relaxed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ had been on the island , but Kotomatas believes its long isolation created favourable conditions . While thousands of prisoners passed through , the human footprint was concentrated , he says , with the camps occupying only a small part of the coastline . Even during the bombing era , disturbance was sporadic and concentrated mainly in the south-east of the island , he adds , away from the areas where monk seals found their refuge . <p> " Seals are adaptable , " says Kotomatas . " I 've been inside a cave while a speedboat passed right by . I could n't hear from the noise , but the seal remained asleep . " <h> Underwater refuge <p> From the speedboat , Antonios Burikas and Ventouris Bountouris scan the water . As officers from Greece 's Natural Environment and Climate Change Agency ( Necca ) , which took over surveillance of Gyaros from WWF in 2023 , their job is to check whether anyone is fishing in the three-nautical-mile protected zone . <p> P. Dendrinos/ MO m <p> An aerial view shows Gyaros ' abandoned prison and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( Credit : P. Dendrinos/ MOm ) <p> Today , the water is quiet . Only two pleasure yachts are anchored in the bay below the prison . The officers politely inform the captains that fishing is not permitted . <p> " More than the patrols themselves , it 's the idea that we are patrolling that deters people , " Burikas says . <p> Sea life around Gyaros had serious advantages long before anyone was actively protecting it . Fishing was banned for safety reasons by the navy , and never systematically opened to large-scale mechanisation . <p> Still , remote and regularly battered by high winds , it is hard to guard from illegal fishing . As the bombing range fell silent in the early 2000s , more boats moved in to exploit waters that had barely been fished for half a century . <p> Constant boat patrols to prevent this was prohibitively expensive , so in 2017 WWF Greece built a remote monitoring system which transmits live feeds to Syros . When a vessel enters the protected zone , officers can dispatch a targeted response . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ says Dimitrios Damalas , a fisheries expert at the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research ( HCMR ) in Anavyssos , Greece . <p> Maria Salomidi , a marine biologist at HCMR who has studied seagrass beds and reefs on Gyaros since 2009 , would see slipper lobsters in impossible numbers as well as giant devil rays , marine turtles , dolphins , whales and monk seals . <p> " When we dive elsewhere , we 'll mostly get out of the water frustrated , " she says . " We see the degradation in the sea . Not in Gyaros ... It 's one of the last heavens on Earth , where you can hear the silence and see the night sky . " <p> In 2015 , researchers from WWF heard a group of Yelkouan shearwaters -- black-and-white seabirds roughly the size of a rock pigeon -- approaching Gyaros at night . It was previously unknown they were even there : the birds were thought likely to be limited to smaller , isolated islets . <p> Long-lived and monogamous , shearwaters return to the same partner and nesting site @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to a single burrow and egg . <p> " One bird can stay on the egg for a week , completely motionless , " says Danae Portolou of the Athens-based Hellenic Ornithological Society , who has been leading efforts to monitor Yelkouan shearwaters in the Aegean Sea . " The other travels , then they switch . " <p> The Gyaros colony is the second largest in the world , accounting for 15% of the global population . It 's precisely the inaccessibility of the islands cracks and crevices -- a habitat untouched by humans -- which has allowed it to thrive . <p> Even here , though , the shearwaters face threats . Introduced rats eat their eggs and chicks -- up to a third of their eggs are lost in this way . Worse still , feral pigs , which dig up burrows and prey on adult birds , have now been illegally introduced . " When a predator targets adults of a long-lived , low-fecundity seabird , the damage is devastating , " says Portolou . <p> Culling of pigs , the more pressing of the two @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ critical , says Portolou . <h> Delicate balance <p> It 's not the only circumstance that is far from perfect on Gyaros . <p> While the seagrass meadows around the island are mostly healthy , the reefs are not . Overfishing elsewhere has removed large predators like groupers and sea bream , meaning smaller fish are overgrazing algal forests , which form the basis of the entire ecosystem . <p> Salomidi 's team is now actively restoring the reefs by planting lab-cultivated algae . Large fish such as groupers and sharks are returning , but many are still immature . " We may need decades to approach something close to a pristine state , " says Damalas . <p> Things are also fragile politically . Even after Gyaros was designated an MPA , local small-scale fishing remained permitted seasonally , under strict conditions . But in 2022 , under pressure from fishing organisations , the government opened the area , leading to a free-for-all which quickly impacted fish and seals . <p> The government soon reversed course , declaring the island a strict no-take zone . Still , scientists remain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . " Fishermen report that boats from other islands arrive at night and on weekends , " says Damalas . " Others feel they have been respecting the rules for nothing . " <p> In April 2026 , a presidential decree , gave the island the highest level of protection and established a permanent legal framework . But experts also stress that Gyaros can not be a stand-alone solution . <p> While Greece has protected 18% of its marine territory , only a small fraction is actively managed . " Even if you protect Gyaros perfectly , if the wider sea is unprotected , the animals remain at risk , " says Kotomatas . " The Mediterranean is one of the most intensively used seas on earth , and pressures from shipping , offshore energy , recreational fishing and marine heatwaves are only increasing . " <p> A proper plan is needed , he says , for how different parts of the sea are used , so fishing , shipping , tourism and conservation do n't end up working against each other . <p> The participatory process used to design @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to follow , says Portolou . " It brought together lots of stakeholders to talk and discuss what they feel Gyaros is for them and what is necessary to be done , " she says . " The process has taken time , but it 's been worthwhile . " <p> In one piece of good news , monk seals are now recovering beyond Gyaros , driven by protection of key habitats and a change in attitudes among fishermen , who no longer dynamite animals in caves , says Kotomatas . <p> As the speedboat turns away from the island , the abandoned prison fades into the distance . Somewhere near the caves below , monk seals nurse their pups on open shores . <p> " Gyaros is an island of hope , " Salomidi says . " But we need a thousand Gyaroses across Greece -- then we might be on to something .

Beyond this clinic 's capacity and specialisations , residents in Finchley and Golders Green must travel to Mary Ward Legal Centre in Holborn ( 9 miles away ) to access support . <p> Such gaps in Legal Aid in any given area have been called " Legal Aid deserts " by the Law Society , who have repeatedly warned that people are struggling to get legal advice when they needed , causing civil cases which could be mediated to end up in county courts . <p> As I have reported from both Croydon County and Bradford County Court , ordinary people who end up in desperate situations -- such as mortgage arrears , a private rental eviction or a dispute with their employer -- often ca n't afford a solicitor and turn up to their local civil court , where waiting lists are spiralling , afraid and uninformed . <p> Judges , clerks and duty solicitors @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Legal Aid was still readily accessible , it 's possible that many of these people would resolve their issues before getting to court . " <p> However , unless you can afford a solicitor or qualify for access to Legal Aid , Sackman knows from her own professional experience that " whether you are bargaining with your employer , trying to leave an abusive relationship , whether you 're a small business trying to claw back a debt that 's owed to you , or challenging an unscrupulous landlord " , it can often feel like those @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we have been ambitious about extending workers ' rights and renters ' rights -- as we should be -- but access to justice is crucial . " <p> The Finchley and Golders Green Free Legal Advice Centre now operates once a month , but Sackman 's team explain that they have been contacted by hundreds of people and could run it far more regularly . <p> " It 's important that we 've taken our free legal advice out into the community , " Sackman says . " This is where people are living their lives . It is not like a law firm model where people would have to come to us ... we 're going to them . State-funded legal aid was established shortly after , introduced via the Legal Aid and Advice Act of 1949 . The goal was to provide " the same level of legal support for the poor " as the NHS @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ financially unable to prosecute or defend their legal rights . <p> Sadly , over time , Legal Aid has been eroded and not upheld as a cornerstone of the accessible state in the same way that the NHS is now regarded . <p> Sackman says that " cutting Legal Aid and cutting access to early legal support is a false economy " . <p> " Having access to early legal help , advice , and advocacy prevents much higher costs down the line , " she adds . <p> Sackman returns to a woman she helped at the Legal Aid clinic in east London early on in her career . . <p> Central to this is the construction and development industry at a time when the government is trying to press ahead with the country 's largest housing expansion for decades . <p> Housebuilders During the growing season , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that naturally grow among the crop . As a low-growing , nitrogen-fixing legume , the lentil enriches the soil while allowing sunlight to reach the native flowers growing nearby . Golden expanses of wild mustard and rapeseed appear first , followed by the intense red of poppies and , when weather conditions permit , the blue of cornflowers together with the violet-pink blossoms of roveja ( wild field pea ) . <p> Harvested between July and August , the petite lentil of Castelluccio di Norcia is prized for its creamy flavour and resilient skin , which holds its shape when cooked . Traditionally , they are cooked in simple soups or served alongside local sausages . <p> Elisabetta Abrami <h> The perfect shot <p> Thanks to social media , the lentil bloom is now one of Italy 's most photographed landscapes . @@139113557 <p> Behind the language of military strategy is a confrontation that risks drawing the wider Middle East into war , says STEVE BISHOP <p> YOU may be spotting bodies of dead bumblebees lying across pavements near you in the summer months . <p> There are several reasons for this , some to do with the weather and some very much due to humans . <p> Bumblebees are social , living in colonies that are maintained by very active workers with a relatively short lifespan of four to six weeks . This means , that in a relatively short space of time , older bees die off and to prevent disease making its way through the colony , the healthy young workers bring out their dead , moving them far away from their colony . <p> Another factor is the weather . It was the warmest June on record in England ( and the second hottest for the whole UK ) in 2026 and other high temperatures are expected this summer . <p> Thermal stress in bees is caused by this kind of extreme heat . Prolonged heat exposure alters development @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ disrupt reproduction , flight capacity and ability to forage . Social insects including bees rely on cooling behaviour for example fanning their wings when things get too hot to buffer the hive but there are limits as to how effective this is in extreme heat . <p> As it gets hotter bee foraging activity may increase , and they may cover greater distances . Bees can thermoregulate themselves by moving heat around their body while in flight , but extremes of temperature can affect their health . <p> Other elements play a part in bee deaths . Pesticide and herbicide use is commonplace and these chemicals affect the fitness of bees , causing them to die off . However , not only do these chemicals affect the bees directly , they can also remove important plants that they rely on for food causing them to starve . Dandelions for example , are a massively important nectar source for bees , but also a plant commonly controlled with herbicides . So do n't weed your garden and pull them out . <p> Pesticide use is one of the historical key causes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ insects feeding on crops -- is somewhat ironically -- responsible for harming a group of animals responsible for their pollination . <p> The EU and Britain have banned the use of the most harmful neonicotinoids , however pesticides are still routinely used , with harmful knock-on effects on pollinators . Insecticides such as organophosphates , synthetic pyrethroids and phenylpyrazoles cause paralysis and death of these insects , as well as disrupting the bees ability to navigate . <p> Habitat loss is another key issue for bees , with land use changing for housing developments , intensive agriculture and other human structures such as roads . Without these habitats to support the bees , their populations suffer . <p> Climate change is causing other problems . <p> Phenological mismatch is when two organisms that are dependent upon each other appear at the wrong time . With a changing climate this is happening . An example of this is that plants that the bees are dependent upon being in flower when the bees are n't around . Essentially they are flowering at a time of year when the bees are n't there @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not have any nectar to feed on , or conversely the flowers could come out before the bees appear . This , of course , is a disaster for both flower and the bees . <p> Insects are the most diverse and abundant group of animals on the planet , but in spite of this dominance they are the most threatened . <p> We are losing our bees at an alarming rate . In Europe , the number of wild bee species considered at risk of extinction has more than doubled from 77 in 2014 to at least 172 today ( around 10 per cent of assessed species ) . <p> But we really need them . They provide so much support for our planet , as decomposers , pest controllers , food for other animals and generally for keeping our systems clean and tidy . Scientists call these these roles ecosystem services . However , one such service they provide is directly very important for us , and disproportionately carried out by one group of insects , the bees , and that is pollination of our crops . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ They support an estimated 75 per cent of global crop pollination , and nearly 90 per cent of all flowering plants . The rest can be pollinated by other animals , or by the wind and weather . <p> If we lose that food security afforded by our pollinators we could have a global food crisis on our hands . <p> When it comes to pesticide use , be a thoughtful and informed consumer . Support local , sustainably produced food where possible and , if feasible , buy from farmers who use nature-friendly practices . This does not necessarily mean choosing organic products , but rather considering how food is produced and the environmental impact of different farming systems . As a homeowner , explore non-chemical alternatives first , and apply any treatments sparingly and responsibly to minimise harm to beneficial insects and other wildlife . <p> One of the simplest ways to address habitat loss for bees is to make room for native species . Plant a diverse range of native flowering species , and leave some areas of lawn unmown . This can help create safe havens @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one thing that people can do to help bees in distress . Providing sugary water to a bee you see struggling on the pavement on a hot summer 's day can help revive it . A mixture of sugar and water will do the trick at a two-to-one ratio of sugar to water . <p> Moving the bee , if safe to do so , to a flower or a shady spot too is also advised . But please do not do this if you have allergies , or are likely to get stung .

@@139122127 <p> Strategy is the quintessential PC genre , keeping us buried in maps , army lists and build orders since the earliest days of PC gaming . But within these broad categories of the genre is a plethora of options , and there are hundreds of dishes that rarely appear on menus outside of Mexico . <p> Most food scholars would agree that at the heart of much of Mexican food tradition is nixtamalization , a labor-intensive , pre-Hispanic process . It involves soaking corn kernels with cal ( calcium hydroxide ) to draw out its nutrients and turning that into the masa needed to make tortillas , tamales and other corn-dough based dishes that are foundational to the cuisine . <p> From Lebanese-influenced dishes , the citrusy flavors of the coastal regions , the almighty torta and the myriad ways that corn can be transformed , here are 23 traditional Mexican dishes that tell the story of this beloved cuisine 's history . <h> Chilaquiles <p> Leftover tortillas find @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ classic dish usually consumed for breakfast , chilaquiles are made with stale tortillas that are cut into strips , fried and tossed in a red or green sauce for a balance of crispy and soft at once . It 's the ultimate utility meal . You 've got a stack of old tortillas leftover from dinner ? Just make chilaquiles . The meal is given a little razzle dazzle with a bit of queso fresco , crema and maybe a runny egg . <p> Looking for a companion to go with your spiced caf ? de olla ? The traditional concha or pan dulce ( sweet bread ) is a beloved option in many Mexican coffee shops and bakeries . The sweet bread roll is airy but sturdy , while the seashell-like topping has a little crunch to it . The confection is often colored pink , yellow , off-white , or in more contemporary spots , in fantastical unicorn pastels . <h> Tecolota <p> Breakfast of champions : A chilaquiles sandwich . <p> Guajillo studio/Adobe Stock <p> Another breakfast option typical of Mexico City , the tecolota takes the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a toasty bolillo roll , filled with refried beans , chilaquiles , along with cheese , crema , a sprinkle of cilantro and diced red onions . <h> Tacos al pastor <p> Al pastor loosely translates to " shepherd-style , " and it 's the basis for a staple offering of taqueros across Mexico . One can trace its roots more than a century ago when Lebanese immigrants brought with them the traditional shawarma spit to Mexico , inspiring a whole way to slow cook meat using an open flame . <p> Here , Mexicans use pork marinated in a blend of chiles , slow-cooked on a trompo or spit . It is often topped with a whole pineapple , whose juices add a tropical hint of flavor to balance the protein 's heat , and is frequently sliced little by little to add a fleck of pineapple garnish atop the taco . <h> Barbacoa <p> Historically , barbacoa references the style of barbecue by the Taino people of the Caribbean . Baja is where one will find the birthplace of the fish taco , said to be influenced by the Japanese who immigrated to Mexico 's Pacific Coast in the early 20th century . Here , white fish filets or cooked shrimp are battered , flash-fried and topped with cabbage or lettuce , pico de gallo and crema . <p> Ceviche is also a common delicacy in coastal regions , in which raw fish or shrimp is cured in citrus juice , accented frequently by sliced rings of jalape @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and served with a tostada or crackers for scooping . <h> Burritos <p> In the north of Mexico , the border town of Ciudad Ju ? rez is the birthplace of the burrito , often derided as an Americanized version of Mexican food but no less authentic . This region of the country is flour tortilla territory . As such , a burrito is made up of a large , flour tortilla filled with just a few ingredients at most , such as carne guisada ( braised beef ) , beans or barbacoa . <p> These burros are rather slender compared with their much thicker relatives -- the Mission-style burrito popularized by chains such as Chipotle . Birria is a spicy meat stew -- traditionally goat but increasingly beef as well -- marinated in guajillo chiles , frequently some sort of citrus such as orange and other ingredients that creates a finger-staining red broth . @@139140309 <p> The incoming prime minister Andy Burnham has said he wants to " end 40 years of neoliberalism " , which saw a " draining away of economic , social and political power " . One of the chief architects of that process was Nigel Lawson . <p> Lawson , an immensely influential figure who held a range of posts in Margaret Thatcher 's government in the 80s , gave away , sold or mismanaged untold swathes of that power . Britain is still paying the price for his mistakes today . <p> " Our policies aimed at a conscious break ... with the entire post-war consensus , " Lawson recounted in his memoir The View from No. 11 , " to change the entire culture of a nation from anti-profits , anti-business , government-dependent lassitude and defeatism , to a pro-profit , pro-business , robustly independent vigour and optimism . " <p> Well that was the rhetoric . Far from being pro-growth , the 1980s witnessed lower growth than the apparently " anti-profits , anti-business " 1970s . And the proceeds of growth from the 1980s was more unequal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ homelessness grew and unemployment soared above three million . <p> And that was just the immediate impact of Lawson and Thatcher 's disastrous policies . Lawson and business secretary Cecil Parkinson believed the City should manage its own affairs through self-regulatory organisations . <p> Consumer and mortgage lending rules were also loosened , and building societies were allowed and encouraged to become banks . Northern Rock was one of the building societies than demutualised to become a bank -- and in 2007 delivered the first bank run in the UK in 150 years , kicking off the banking crash from which the UK economy has yet to recover . <p> In 2010 a contrite Lawson told Radio 4 that the UK banking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reforms " . " <p> That phrase sums up Lawson 's policies -- business wins , the taxpayer loses . To play a fair part in tackling climate change , the UK would need to reduce emissions by 13 per cent per year -- and deploy " timely technologies " , including retrofitting homes , " like the reconstruction of Europe after the second world war " . <p> To assess the government 's plan , and the response to it by the labour movement and social movements , here I look at seven interlocking problems . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heat pumps , in response to the disastrous failures of previous schemes ; then the continuing absence of effective regulation , and failure to create conditions for a workforce trained and rewarded for the task ; the danger that landlords in the private rented sector will use retrofit schemes further to bully and exploit tenants ; a failure of regulation and training for heat pump installation ; the mismatch of gas and electricity prices in corporate-dominated energy markets that obstruct electrification ; the lack of coordinated , place-based approaches to retrofit , exacerbated by the hollowing out of local government and direct labour organisations ; and the government 's housing policy , focused on persuading developers and construction companies to build new stock , instead of undoing the damage done by decades of marketisation , including to insulation and heating . <p> To develop an approach that both drives out fossil fuels and reverses decades of mounting inequality in housing , the labour movement and social movements should take all these aspects into account . <p> Retrofit is the ABC of decarbonisation in the UK , where most houses are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is the most poorly insulated in northern Europe . So , even though heat pumps convert electricity to heat energy more than three times as efficiently as boilers convert gas to heat energy , a heat pump still may not be cheaper to run than a boiler . <p> Fuel poverty campaigners have long demanded price reform . And even the government 's own Climate Change Committee says policy costs ( items related to renewables investment guarantees and other policy decisions ) should be removed from electricity bills , to make electricity cheaper in comparison to gas . <p> The problem runs deeper , though . UK wholesale electricity prices are set so that all power generators receive the price of the most expensive kilowatt-hour bought that day : this ties the wholesale prices of cheap-to-generate renewables power to gas prices and reinforces retail buyers ' vulnerability to volatile international fossil fuel markets . To defend ourselves from all this means to reverse decades of neoliberalism and fossil fuel companies ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the setting of retail prices in the public interest , for example by means of a single , publicly owned buyer of wholesale electricity . <p> HOW THE JOBS GET DONE <p> The travesty of past retrofit schemes was " not simply a story of inadequate oversight or accountability " , Pauker argues ; rather , trying to deliver high-quality retrofit through subsidies to contractors who are " structurally incentivised to minimise costs " made widespread failure almost inevitable . The WHP is , in one respect , a step forward . Instead of funding decarbonisation through the ' supplier obligation ' on energy companies -- who raise the money from customers ' bills , penalising the poorest -- the state will pay grants itself out of general taxation . <p> The money will still be spent unequally , though : while ? 4.4 billion will go to low-income homes for the most urgently needed upgrades , most of a ? 5.3-billion Warm Homes Fund and a ? 2.7-billion boiler upgrade scheme will go in grants and loans to better-off households . Often they will have to add their own @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Neoliberal ideology pervades the plan . It is presented not as a collective challenge in the face of climate emergency , or as public action to meet social need , but as an " offer to consumers " . Campaigners have long insisted that housing will never be transformed on the scale required without empowering local government to coordinate the work -- and they welcome the greater role for mayoral authorities and local councils envisaged in the WHP . But the government has no intention of reversing the long-term trend towards outsourcing work to contractors or the obliteration of councils ' direct labour organisations . <p> Evidence is clearly documented that public bodies such as the Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund work more effectively than contractors , and that public schemes can better integrate retrofit with other home improvements and achieve economies of scale . So far , it is being ignored . <p> Ellen Robottom of the Greener Jobs Alliance told The Ecologist : " To meet a challenge at this scale , we need a retrofit programme that is free at the point of installation . " <p> HOUSING POLICY <p> The deep flaws in the WHP can only be understood in the context of the government 's signature policy of building 1.5 million new homes -- which housing researchers say , despite some welcome funding for social housing , will not solve the problems caused by decades of marketisation . In writing this part I have , especially , learned from : UCL IIPP , Homes that Do n't Cost the Earth , ' Taking Stock : A Foundation for Future Housing Strategy ' ( June 2025 ) ; and Nick Bano , Against Landlords : How to Solve the Housing Crisis ( Verso , April 2025 ) . <p> The government 's housing policy relies heavily on large-volume private sector developers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ best use of the existing housing stock . The damage done by decades of policy aimed at turning homes into financial assets -- the rundown of social housing , the expansion of the private rented sector , the relentless increase of rents and mortgages -- will not be undone . Where in the 1970s the state directly funded council housing , it now transfers billions each year to private landlords via housing benefit . <p> This grand capitulation to private wealth means that the UK 's housing stock is used inefficiently . Housing has become less affordable not because there is an underlying shortage of space , but because the space is used inefficiently . One third of households in England have two or more spare bedrooms , but financial disincentives make it difficult or impossible for those who wish to downsize to do so . <p> Well-researched solutions to the housing crisis -- rent controls , the transfer of homes from the private rented sector to social housing , incentives for downsizing -- are ignored by a government deeply wedded to neoliberal ' market principles ' . This is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are sidelined . Circular construction practices and efficient use of residentially zoned land are too . Energy efficiency requirements for newbuilds are far from what they could be with modern building techniques and what they are in other European countries . <p> WHAT TO DO ? <p> Our homes are central to how we live , and the need to change the way they are heated is central to tackling climate breakdown . Decarbonisation , by way of retrofitting insulation and installing heat pumps and solar panels , could and should be a powerful theme to unify action on climate with action for social justice . It is no surprise , then , that a wide swathe of civil society -- from tenants ' and housing rights organisations and fuel poverty campaigners to climate activists and trade unionists -- has responded forcefully to the government 's plans . <p> It is vital , and difficult , to take an integrated view of the problems . However , as far as I can see there is as yet no unifying force able to bring all these campaigning efforts together . There @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ view . In the 20th century , the labour movement 's aspirations were voiced politically through the Labour party . But 40 years of neoliberal reaction have not only produced the interlocking problems listed above -- through marketisation of housing and energy supply , degradation of local government , ruination of public construction capacity and training -- but also destroyed social democracy in its 20th-century form . <p> The current Labour government stands stubbornly for enforcement of neoliberal norms . Many of the campaign proposals mentioned above are effectively calls to restore bits of the social democratic gains of the late 20th century , from building industry regulation and restraints on exploitative landlords to public provision via local government . <p> How , and whether , such reversals can be achieved in the context of 21st-century capitalism , bent on further concentration of wealth and haunted by climate breakdown , is an open question . That is not offered as a reason to despair , but as an assessment of the difficulties we need to overcome . With this in mind , there is every reason to believe that we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so obviously necessary to tackle climate breakdown and social injustice . <p> This Author <p> Dr Simon Pirani is honorary professor at the University of Durham , a life member of the National Union of Journalists , and author of books on energy systems , Russia and Ukraine . @@139153105 <h> Britain must tackle climate migration before people reach the border <p> Too often , political debate about migration begins with a boat , a border crossing or an asylum claim . <p> But when Abdihakiin Hassan Jiirow gave his testimony to our recent APPG inquiry on Climate Change and Migration , he did not offer such a simple explanation for how and why people move . He described drought and the loss of livestock ; he spoke of flooding , insecure shelter , food shortages and scarce clean water ; he talked about interrupted schooling , and persistent violence from militias and non-state actors . <p> For him and for many others , those pressures accumulated until the conditions necessary for ordinary life had broken down . At that point , remaining at home was no longer a meaningful choice . His testimony should change how we discuss climate migration . <p> That is the central argument of Before the Border , the new report from the All-Party Parliamentary Group for Climate , Nature and Security . It is also why the government 's new Climate Security Taskforce must @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ risks and act before crisis becomes displacement . <p> Climate change does not operate as a single trigger sending people directly towards Britain . It acts through systems . Drought , flooding , extreme heat and environmental degradation interact with poverty , conflict , weak governance and failing infrastructure . <p> Movement is usually internal or regional . People travel first to the nearest town , city or neighbouring country where they hope to find safety , employment or essential services . <p> The principal security threat is not the person who moves . It is the unmanaged systems failure that removed their choices . <p> Our evidence also showed what can happen when some of those choices are restored . Ahmad Ouwier arrived in Jordan as a Syrian refugee . He moved from informal work into information technology and entrepreneurship , founded a business , and created opportunities for refugees and Jordanian citizens . <p> His story shows that resilience depends upon institutions as much as individuals . Ability and ambition can still be frustrated by restrictions on documentation , lawful work , education , finance and company registration @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about displaced young Syrians . They do not want to remain permanently defined by vulnerability or treated solely as recipients of aid . They want education , skills , lawful employment that facilitates agency and ability to further the social and economic future of the country hosting them -- the opportunity to potentially contribute rather than permanently consume . <p> These testimonies illustrate two paths . Where institutions collapse , displacement can become prolonged , destabilising and intergenerational . Where people retain access to education , water , lawful work , finance and functioning local government , mobility can become a form of adaptation - a means of rebuilding lives and strengthening receiving communities . <p> This is not only a humanitarian issue . It is a matter of preventive security . <p> Britain already possesses expertise across government , the intelligence community , local authorities and universities . What it lacks is a permanent mechanism capable of combining that knowledge , identifying where climate pressures are converging with fragility and translating warning into action . <p> It should identify where pressures on water , food , livelihoods , infrastructure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assess those already displaced , but also those trapped because they lack the resources to move . Every warning should be linked to a practical policy choice -- diplomatic engagement , adaptation finance , humanitarian assistance or conflict prevention . <p> This capability must work with countries , not impose solutions upon them . The climate security intelligence model developed with Jordan and funded by the UK Foreign , Commonwealth and Development Office demonstrates the value of nationally owned systems combining environmental data with local knowledge and political analysis . <p> Satellite data can reveal rainfall decline , vegetation loss or rising temperatures . It can not explain whether a family will adapt , move , become vulnerable to exploitation or lose faith in the state . Effective warning requires both data and human judgement . <p> Britain must also recognise its own exposure . Flooding , coastal erosion , extreme heat and infrastructure disruption will increasingly affect where people can live and whether receiving communities can absorb internal movement . Managed retreat and local resilience are now matters of national preparedness . <p> Migration policy will remain necessary . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ begins its response only when people reach a border has begun too late . <p> The risks posed by climate change and ecological collapse have been recognised in the National Security Assessment ; and the new Climate Security Taskforce is a very positive move . Government now needs to establish a permanent warning capability , and the financial strategy and parliamentary accountability required to turn awareness into action . <p> Climate change is already reshaping mobility . The question is whether Britain will manage the consequences intelligently and early , or continue paying more to confront them after prevention has failed . <p> Barry Gardiner is Labour MP for Brent West and chair of the APPG on Climate Nature and Security , and Prof Tim Clack is an associate fellow of the Centre for Historical &amp; Armed Conflict Research

@@139170354 <p> On The Road USA is complete . Over the last 49 days I have travelled from Seattle to Maine , down to Atlanta , back to Boston and on to New York City . There was one domestic flight thanks to England being good at international major tournaments now , but this was a 7,835-mile driving epic to most corners of America . I went to 10 per cent of the matches at a World Cup , going to 10 different stadiums . <p> And this is the ultimate result : 101 things I learned from a monstrous journey -- across US cities and small towns , through vast deserts and forests , meeting people along the way and taking in a World Cup like no other . Strap in : <p> 1 ) The one thing that surprised me more than anything else on this trip was the welcoming nature of small towns in Texas and other southern states . I heard warnings of a mistrust of outsiders and the type of atmosphere that would make me fearful . I experienced precisely none of that . These places @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ met all summer . <p> 2 ) While this was true everywhere in the USA , it is important for me to also say : I was in a position of privilege . I am white , I am male , I am cisgender and I am a UK tourist ( and Americans love nothing more than a UK tourist ) . My experience would not necessarily be shared by others and I am not intending to speak for everyone . <p> 3 ) For all the relevant concerns ( and I had plenty of my own ) , the USA generally pulled this off . The tickets and transport were disgustingly expensive and priced out regular match-going supporters , but the stadiums were full after the first few games , the atmospheres good and the use of Mexican waves mercifully abated after the first week . <p> 4 ) This was aided hugely by something I have never seen at a major tournament before : vast swathes of Americans with match tickets seemingly picking one of the teams to support rather than watching on as entirely neutral observers . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ thousands of miles away , but it dramatically improved atmospheres at matches . <p> 5 ) And then Donald Trump ruined the vibe around the US national team and the World Cup in general with his boasting about intervening to get Folarin Balogun 's suspension suspended . Hearing Marco Rubio say " this is why the Fifa trophy has been in this office for so long " is one of those moments that should define the next age of Fifa . It wo n't . <p> 6 ) One of the great stereotypes of the USA is that it is all fast food restaurants , to which I say : yes , there really are a lot of fast food restaurants . The list of chain places where you can get a regular burger ( and I will have left loads out ) : McDonald 's , Burger King , Dairy Queen , Carl 's Jr , Arby 's , White Castle , Five Guys , Hardee 's , Wendy 's , Denny 's , Whataburger , In-N-Out Burger , Shake Shack , Culver 's , Cook Out , Red @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , IHOP . <p> I 've not even touched upon chicken , pizzas or Mexican food . The choice blows your mind . <p> 7 ) But it 's also thick to say that fast food is the only option , which some people assume because of the sheer choice . The immigrant food culture is America 's greatest asset for a traveller . You can walk into pretty much any small town and find options for Mexican , Korean and Chinese food that you 'd be delighted with in any UK city , and the average level of quality is astounding . <p> 8 ) Foreign travellers often moan about tipping culture in the US , but it is also the best country for customer service that I have ever visited . Part of that is the reward element of high tips , but it 's absolutely not only that . <p> You can walk into a fuel station ( where there are no tips ) in the middle of nowhere from Oregon to Maine and you will almost never not receive a more friendly interaction that you will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . They 're just ... friendlier in customer-facing positions . <p> 9 ) Actually , I 'm just extending that to all American people . Some may find the " Have a nice day " and " Missing you already " sugary friendliness a bit much , but I am not one of those people . When you are spending almost every day for seven weeks seeing nobody you know , being treated like a long-lost friend by a waitress is a real boost . <p> 10 ) The lane discipline of American drivers on highways is really something to behold . Are you happy to drive two miles an hour below the speed limit in the outside lane of four simply because the road is long and the concentration levels low ? Then move to the USA . <p> 11 ) You have a vision of USA summer weather that is largely curated by television shows you 've seen in England that all happen to be set in California . In fact , in a world increasingly affected by climate change , a large number of states cycle between @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ you never want to go outside again . <p> 12 ) You have never known panic until you are 20 minutes from getting into your car to drive for six hours across three states and your phone pings with a tornado alert that you did n't ask for . <p> 13 ) If I had one wish in my life , it would be for someone to love me as much as American towns love an absolutely massive flag on an absolutely massive pole . You could wrap a small office building in some of these . <p> 14 ) There were watch parties for every USA game in whichever town or city I was in at the time , but I saw very few USMNT shirts between games . The striped kit was held up as a design classic , but that does n't seem to have dripped down to smalltown USA . <p> 15 ) But the one shirt you really could see everywhere during the World Cup was the white Mexico away shirt . It reinforces how -- and this is absolutely a sweeping statement -- soccer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It 's that exercise is more of an organised activity . @@139195850 <p> The combined water level in two of the United States ' biggest reservoirs , Lake Powell and Lake Mead , has fallen to a historic low , in what experts are calling a significant moment in the Colorado River crisis -- threatening a water system that supplies tens of millions . <p> On July 12 , Lake Powell was at 3,524 feet and Lake Mead was just under 1,043 feet , breaking a record set in March 2023 , according to an analysis published by five Colorado River experts last week . Together , the two reservoirs have n't been this low since 1957 , during the construction of the Glen Canyon Dam , before Lake Powell even existed . <p> It 's " a milestone in the history of water storage in the Colorado River Basin , " said Jack Schmidt , director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University and an author on the analysis . The record reveals " the seriousness of the uniquely small amount of water that is presently stored in the basin 's reservoirs , " he added . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Colorado River , on July 14 , 2026 , in Page , Arizona . <p> John Locher/AP <p> The Colorado River is the lifeblood of the Southwest . It irrigates more than 5 million acres of farmland , generates enough electricity to power around 700,000 homes and provides water for 40 million people . <p> The headwaters of this 1,400-mile long artery are in the Rocky Mountains , fed by melting snowpack . The river flows across seven states , filling Lake Powell and Lake Mead as it winds toward the Gulf of California . The two lakes , which are essentially one gigantic reservoir separated by the Grand Canyon , hold just under 60% of the total water currently stored in thebasin . <p> The Colorado River has shrunk rapidly over the past 25 years as water demand has boomed and climate change has delivered hotter , drier weather and dwindling snow . Today , 95% of the basin is in drought . <p> Levels in both lakes have fallen further since the record was first set last week . Lake Powell , currently 23% full , is at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ based on current rates of decline , could reach its all-time record low sometime next month . Lake Mead is 27% full and less than a foot from its all-time record low , set in July 2022 . <p> People ride a golf cart beneath a protruding dock used during higher water levels at the Antelope Point Marina on Lake Powell , July 14 , 2026 , near Page , Arizona . <p> John Locher/AP <p> The researchers predict Lake Mead and Lake Powell will set a new record low for their combined water storage every day from now until next spring , when the runoff from the winter snowpack starts to replenish water levels . <p> Lake Powell could fall so low by spring 2027 that it reaches " minimum power pool " level , meaning its dam will no longer be able to generate hydropower , according to a July report from the Bureau of Reclamation . <p> This report " highlights the ongoing vulnerability of the Colorado River system and reinforces the urgent need for updated guidelines and procedures , " said a Reclamation spokesperson . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The low reservoir levels are a dramatic signal that the system is at risk of crashing , meaning reservoir levels so low that water can not be delivered from them , " said Sarah Porter , director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University . <p> It may influence the fraught negotiations between the seven states on how to share the Colorado River 's diminishing water . <p> Under the 1922 Colorado River compact , the four states in the Upper Colorado River Basin ( Colorado , New Mexico , Utah and Wyoming ) are allotted 7.5 million acre-feet of water every year and another 7.5 million goes to the three in the Lower basin ( California , Arizona and Nevada ) . <p> The shrinking river means states are going to have to accept less , but how this works in practice has yet to be ironed out . A federally-imposed February deadline for states to agree came and went with no deal . <p> The negotiations are complex , Porter said . States are being asked " to agree to deep cuts and potentially @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ back to their states and ' sell ' to their water users and decision makers . " But , she added , " the new low may be a catalyst . " <p> On Tuesday , Interior Secretary Doug Burgum held a virtual meeting with governors of the seven basin states to address the state of the Colorado River . @@139242943 <h> Bumblebees are struggling in UK heatwaves - but you can help them <p> UK bumblebees could suffer sharp falls in their numbers as heatwaves become more frequent and intense , new analysis suggests . <p> The findings - shared exclusively with the BBC - draw on data from the Bumblebee Conservation Trust 's long-running national monitoring scheme , which shows a decline in populations after the record-breaking heat of 2022 . <p> The warning comes as Britain emerges from a third heatwave in as many months , with temperatures in the range where bumblebees can struggle to fly without overheating . <p> Bumblebees are not just one of the best-loved sights of the British summer , they are also vital pollinators , helping sustain wildflowers and some of the crops we rely on . <p> The impact of heatwaves is two-fold for bumblebees . <p> UK species are adapted to our historically cooler climate - with fat , furry bodies that help them retain heat and powerful flight muscles that warm them as they fly . <p> But in a heatwave their muscles generate more heat , while their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ down . <p> Dr Richard Comont , the Trust 's science manager , says that once air temperatures reach around 28C to 32C , UK bumblebees can start to struggle to fly without overheating . If they can not fly , they can not forage . <p> The BeeWalk data shows in 2022 , when the UK had three official summer heatwaves and temperatures reached 40.3C , population numbers dropped significantly . <p> Red-tailed , buff-tailed and common carder bumblebees - three of the country 's most common species - peaked well below normal levels - down 20% , 25% and 35% respectively - before dropping further into autumn as colonies struggled . <p> The effects appeared to last beyond that summer . BeeWalk data showed overall queen numbers were below average in March , April and May 2023 . <h> To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser . <p> This video can not be played <p> Figure caption , <p> UK 's Climate Editor , Justin Rowlatt , explains how the UK 's bumblebees are fighting a battle on many fronts during heatwaves <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bad for bumblebees . Previous warm years have been good for some species , particularly those with more southerly ranges . <p> The problem is extreme heat and drought . As well as their overheating bodies , the other issue for bumblebees is dwindling supplies of food . <p> Colonies depend on workers bringing back a steady supply of nectar and pollen through the summer . If flowering plants begin to dry up , they produce less . <p> Dr Paul Williams , a bumblebee expert at the Natural History Museum , says foraging is an energy calculation for bumblebees . The nectar return has to make the expenditure of energy worthwhile . As he puts it , they need to " make a profit " . <p> They can not afford to waste energy searching dried-up flowers for nectar and pollen that is no longer there . <p> If they can not find enough food , larvae develop more slowly , colonies grow less strongly and fewer new queens may be produced for the following year . <p> Rising global temperatures , as a result of climate change , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ intense heatwaves . <h> What can you do to help the bumblebees ? <p> Conservationists say the best way to help is by creating more flower-rich habitats , so bumblebees can find food even as the climate becomes more extreme . <p> Dr Sarah Beynon is an insect expert whose west Wales farm is managed for wildlife as well as food . She has planted meadows , willows , hedgerows , tussocky grasses and late-flowering crops to give insects food through the summer . <p> " When we came , this farm was a wildlife desert , " she says . " In 10 years , it 's become a nature reserve . " <p> Her message is that people do not need acres of land to help . A pot of native wildflowers on a doorstep or windowsill can act as a small refuelling stop for insects moving through a human-dominated landscape . <p> " Your flowerpot is a service station , " she says . " It 's somewhere to rest , refuel and carry on . " <p> Dr Richard Comont adds that putting in a pond @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Flowers growing near water tend to produce nectar with more moisture in it , he says . Bumblebees can not collect water in the way honeybees do , they get most of the liquid they need from nectar , so wetter nectar can help make colonies more resilient in hot weather . <p> Whilst planting dense shrubs gives bumblebees places to escape the heat of the sun , and can allow them to move between flowers through cooler patches of air .

Two weeks ago , 16% of French rivers were reported to have dried up . In Vernon , Normandy , the flow of the Seine has dropped from an average of 200 cubic metres per second in July last year to 110 . <p> Despite a rainy winter that caused flooding , the sweltering heat this summer and low rainfall since April has created an extreme drought , sucking rivers across Europe dry . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ departments are under water restrictions , and a state of emergency has been declared in 58 of them . There 's theatre , comedy , literature , poetry , dance , wellbeing and family activities , creating something that appeals to people of all ages and interests . <p> Secondly , it 's the audience . The people who come to Latitude have helped shape its identity over the years . There 's a wonderful atmosphere , with families , friends and generations enjoying the festival together . <p> Finally , there 's the location . Festivals develop a unique relationship with where they 're held . Glastonbury belongs in Glastonbury , Reading belongs in Reading , the Isle of Wight Festival belongs on the Isle of Wight and Latitude belongs at Henham Park . Reading and Leeds are wonderful examples of that . <p> From the very beginning , my ambition was for Latitude to establish itself for the long term . I 'm incredibly proud that , 20 years on , it has become such an important part of Britain 's cultural calendar and continues to evolve whilst staying true to what made it special in the first place . <p> What was your first job ? <p> My first job was when I was eight years old . They were n't something people with mortgages and families generally went to ; they tended to attract those living a more alternative lifestyle . <p> It 's extraordinary to see how much that has changed . decline in river levels and growing pressure on groundwater sources across the wider region . <p> It extends restrictions already in place in Kent since July 3 , bringing the total number of customers , introduced in July 2025 , was not lifted until February 2026 , raising fears locally that this year 's restrictions could run for many months if the weather does not turn . <p> Brighton and Hove City Council maintains 147 parks and green spaces across the city , including heritage sites such as Brunswick , Palmeira , and Regency Squares . <p> None of these public lawns are irrigated as a matter of routine , meaning they are entirely dependent on rainfall -- and with July historically the driest month of the year in Brighton , averaging only around 50mm of rain compared with other months , an extended dry spell hits ornamental grass particularly hard . <p> Brighton and Hove 's brown squares are a visible symptom of a much larger problem . <p> The Environment Agency 's National @@139275070 <h> Brighton and Hove e-scooter trial can transform city travel <p> This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today , and has been written by our American colleagues . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> This week marks an exciting milestone for Brighton and Hove as we launch our new e-scooter hire trial . <p> For many years , our city has been at the forefront of sustainable transport . Whether it 's walking , cycling , public transport or our popular bike hire scheme , we 've consistently looked for innovative ways to help people move around the city safely , affordably and sustainably . The launch of our e-scooter trial is the latest step on that journey and one that I 'm incredibly pleased to see become a reality . <p> The trial means residents , commuters and visitors will now have access to a convenient new transport option that can help make many everyday journeys easier . With e-scooters available from hubs along the seafront , in the city centre and at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ able to connect quickly with key destinations across the city . <p> We 've also ensured free minute bundles are available for jobseekers and recipients of Universal Credit . <p> Importantly , this is not simply about introducing a new mode of transport ; it 's about giving people more choice in how they travel . We know that many short journeys currently made by car could instead be completed using more sustainable forms of transport . By adding e-scooters to the range of options available , we are making it easier for people to leave the car at home and choose cleaner ways to get around our city . <p> Reducing the number of short car journeys helps to cut congestion on our roads , particularly at busy times of day . Fewer vehicles on the road can also contribute to improved air quality and lower carbon emissions , supporting the city 's wider ambitions to tackle climate change and create healthier communities . As a compact city where many journeys are relatively short , Brighton &amp; Hove is particularly well-suited to an e-scooter hire scheme . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ train can use e-scooters to travel between attractions , shopping areas and seafront destinations , while residents can make quick and affordable journeys for work , education or leisure . Better connections between different forms of transport help create a more accessible and vibrant city for everyone . <p> What often surprises people is that e-scooters can also deliver benefits for both physical and mental well-being . <p> While e-scooters are electrically powered , riding them still requires balance , coordination , concentration and active engagement with your surroundings . They can encourage people to spend more time outdoors , helping them integrate active travel into their daily routines . For some people who may not feel able to cycle longer distances or tackle the city 's hills , e-scooters can provide an accessible way to enjoy travelling actively and independently . <p> There are also mental health benefits . Travelling in the open air , avoiding stressful traffic queues and feeling connected to your surroundings can make journeys more enjoyable and less pressured . For many users in other parts of the country , e-scooters have become a practical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , while we are enthusiastic about the opportunities e-scooters present , we are equally clear that safety must come first . <p> That is why we have worked hard to ensure Brighton &amp; Hove 's trial includes some of the most robust safety measures seen anywhere in the country . The scheme has been carefully designed following extensive public consultation , consideration of residents ' feedback and lessons learned from trials operating in more than 50 towns and cities across the UK . <p> Only people aged 18 or over who hold at least a provisional driving licence can hire an e-scooter . The vehicles are speed-limited to 12.5mph , below the maximum speed permitted under national trial rules . They are fitted with lights and registration plates , while GPS technology ensures they can not be used in designated no-go areas . <p> Let me be absolutely clear on another important point , private e-scooters remain illegal to use on public roads , pavements , cycle lanes and other public spaces . This trial provides a legal , regulated and controlled alternative that allows us to test the benefits @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> As the trial progresses , we will monitor usage data , safety information and public feedback closely . Reviews will take place throughout the trial period , allowing us to understand what works well and where improvements may be needed . <p> This launch is the beginning of an important new chapter for transport in Brighton &amp; Hove . By embracing innovation while putting safety first , we have an opportunity to encourage more sustainable travel , reduce congestion , improve air quality and give people another enjoyable way to move around our city . <p> I 'm excited to see the trial get underway and look forward to seeing how residents and visitors make use of this new addition to Brighton &amp; Hove 's transport network . Together , we can continue building a cleaner , healthier and more sustainable city for the future . <p> Councillor Trevor Muten is Cabinet member for Transport and City Infrastructure at Brighton &amp; Hove City Council <h> Useful Links <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . @@139284362 <p> On the high-altitude plains of Tibet , ringed by snowy mountains and buffeted by harsh winds , scientists are hard at work creating horned , fluffy clones . <p> These are Tibetan yaks , designed and cloned in secretive labs more than 4,000 meters above sea level , where researchers hope to create an " elite " herd of super-yaks , healthier and more fertile than their predecessors . <p> This project , scientists hope , could even potentially revive a wild species revered by local Tibetans as a favorite of the land god . <p> The long-haired Himalayan cattle are a critical part of the region 's economy and culture . But both domestic yaks and their wild cousins have been facing threats for years , with some rare subspecies at risk of disappearing entirely . <p> Authorities in the southwestern Chinese region have poured tens of millions of dollars into boosting the yak industry in recent years -- and they hope cloning can help . <p> The first yak clone came in July 2025 , Chinese state media hailing it as a breakthrough achievement that combined cloning @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- and researchers are now aiming to create a herd of more than 100 " elite " yak clones by 2028 , boasting desired traits like faster growth and larger size . <p> " This shows the technology has moved from a one-time success to a stable , mass-scale application , " said Fang Shengguo , the project 's scientific lead and director of the State Conservation Center for Gene Resources of Endangered Wildlife , according to state-run news agency Xinhua . <p> But the project , which is supported by the Tibetan government , has also raised concerns among international observers . Cloning remains highly controversial , especially recent " de-extinction " projects , which gained global attention for trying to bring back long-dead species . <p> Many experts acknowledge there are legitimate arguments for using cloning in conservation , and for gene selection in farming . But the ethical waters are murky , and any such project should have high levels of public transparency and accountability , said Lisa Moses , a veterinarian and bioethicist at Harvard Medical School . <p> CNN reached out multiple times to Fang @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Zhejiang University ; China 's State Council Information Office ; and the Tibet Autonomous Region Information Office . All of them either referred requests to other authorities or never responded . <p> A wild yak is seen near the Zangser Kangri Glacier at the Changtang National Nature Reserve in Tibet on March 12 . <p> Sonam Jamcan/Xinhua/Getty Images <h> Yak to the future <p> First off , there are two main types of yaks in Tibet -- and the cloning project has different goals for them . <p> There are wild yaks , which face the risk of extinction and are protected under Chinese law . Their numbers have declined by more than a third in the last 30 years , with just 10,000 to 20,000 individuals left , according to the Wildlife Conservation Society . <p> Then we have their smaller cousin , the domestic yak , which is not endangered and numbers roughly 14 million worldwide , the vast majority in the rarefied air of the Tibetan plateaus . They 're a backbone of Tibet 's economy , used by nomadic farmers for wool , milk , meat @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A white yak in Nam Tso Lake ( Nam Co ) in the Nyainqentanglha mountains of Tibet . <p> Sergi Reboredo/VW Pics/Universal Images/Getty Images <p> A herder collects yaks ' milk at the grasslands along Nam Tso Lake ( Nam Co ) , on June 26 , 2025 , in Lhasa , Tibet . <p> Gongga Laisong/China News Service/VCG/Getty Images <p> Both species are threatened by climate change and habitat degradation , with warmer temperatures bringing invasive plant species and increased competition for resources -- a big problem in one of the world 's most inhospitable terrains . <p> " In the plateaus , it is just a fragile ecosystem , and with climate change , you have more extreme weather . It could wipe out entire herds in a particular area if you have a really bad winter storm , " said Carol Chyau , founder of SHOKAY , a yak's-wool clothing brand that works directly with conservation organizations and Tibetan communities . <p> There 's also the problem of inbreeding and cross-breeding . Wild yaks cross-breed with domestic yaks , which shrinks their wild genetic pool ; and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ genetic pool . Even within the same species , unchecked inbreeding has harmed genetic diversity and overall health , experts say . <p> Over the past decade , yaks ' body size and weight have gone down , as well as their fertility -- with just a 20% success rate in natural reproduction and fertilization , said Fang , the lead scientist , in a news release by Zhejiang University last year . " Human activity and ecological changes have led to a severe degradation crisis for the yak population . " <p> Cloning , he hopes , can offer a solution . <h> How to clone your yak <p> The remote research base in Damxung , Tibet , where scientists are breeding and cloning yaks.Xinhua <p> Here 's how you make a clone : First , scientists select the strongest , healthiest yaks as DNA donors . As of June , all the clone calves are " growing healthily , " according to media reports . <p> Chinese researchers say this approach could bring major economic benefits to the domestic yak industry . For one , it 's much faster than natural reproduction , said a separate news release by Zhejiang University in March . Yaks breed notoriously slowly , with females birthing just four or five offspring in their lifetime -- a major challenge for their long-term survival . <p> And while yaks are already uniquely adapted to their tough environment -- with thick fleeces for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scientists can choose yak donors with " the best genetic traits " to breed clones with higher fertility , better disease resistance , and stronger resilience , said the university . @@139284382 <p> When astrobiologist Adam Frank walked into the office of NASA scientist Gavin Schmidt , he had what he believed was the weirdest question : do aliens experience climate change ? It took just moments for Schmidt to out-weird him . <p> Frank , a University of Rochester professor who looks for signs of life in the universe , was digging into whether advanced civilizations would inevitably trigger climate shifts , just as humans are doing now . He was looking at other planets , he told Schmidt that day back in 2017 , " because , of course , we know that there have been no other civilizations on Earth . " <p> Schmidt immediately cut him off . " How do you know that ? " he asked . <p> It was a record scratch moment , Frank said , and it started the two scientists off on an investigation . If an advanced civilization had lived on Earth millions of years ago , powered themselves with energyand wiped themselves out , would we know ? Would they have left traces of their presence etched into the record @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Silurian hypothesis " -- after a fictional advanced race of reptiles in the TV show " Doctor Who " -- and published a paper on it in 2018 . <p> It is a mind-bending idea that not only looks deep into the Earth 's past but also far into its future , as humans change the climate swiftly and dramatically by burning fossil fuels . " It is a thought experiment , but one that exposes our potential vulnerability globally , " said Katharine Hayhoe , an atmospheric scientist at Texas Tech University , who was not involved in the research . <p> The Silurean hypothesis opens big questions about the trajectory of advanced civilizations and whether all those that harness energy on a global scale are destined to burn out , or whether there 's a chance to live sustainably and survive for millions of years . <p> " These questions are all relevant to exactly the moment that we 're in , " said Frank . " We are pushing the planet into a new climate regime ... we know this is true , right ? And @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> A Silurian , a fictional character from the TV show " Doctor Who , " which was part of an advanced race of reptiles that pre-dated humans . <p> Everett Collection <p> The reason Schmidthad been mulling the possibility of previous advanced civilizations on Earth was an event deep in the past . <p> Around 55 million years ago , the planet 's climate signals went haywire . Global temperatures spiked up to 15 degrees Fahrenheit and ecosystems collapsed , as huge amounts of planet-heating carbon were injected into the atmosphere . <p> This period , known as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum and first noted in the 1990s , may have been the result of an enormous volcanic eruption , or maybe a sudden release of methane.But exactly why it happened is still something of a mystery . What intrigued Schmidt were the similarities to what 's happening now as humans push up temperatures and drive extinctions . <p> And it 's not the only unexplained change deep in the planet 's past that echoes our present , other periods have seen oceans starved of oxygen and sharp hikes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate events , but what if they were n't ? How would we know ? In their report , Frank and Schmidt go through the chain of possible evidence that might exist in support of a past advanced civilization . <p> Today , only around 1% of the Earth 's surface is urbanized and it would n't take long for what we 've built to be erased . The further back in time a hypothetical civilization existed , the harder it would be to find direct evidence , like objects . <p> Over millions of years , the planet is resculpted as tectonic plates shift , volcanoes erupt and land erodes . The Earth 's oldest large-scale stretch of land is the Negev Desert in southern Israel , at around 1.8 million years old . <p> Sand dunes in bright sun in the Negev Desert , Israel . This is the oldest large-scale stretch of land on Earth . <p> Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images <p> Surface features may not provide much evidence , so the scientists looked at fossils . A vanishingly small fraction of animal species is fossilized , however @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Earth for about 180 million years , but only a few thousand near-complete fossils have been discovered . <p> It might be easy to miss a civilization that only existed for 100,000 years , a mere blip in the 400-million-year-old history of complex life on the planet . <p> The researchersthen considered traces left by chemical changes . Think of the Grand Canyon , Frank said , where you can see line after line representing different ages of the Earth . " Every one of those strata is ground up rock that keeps a memory of what the chemistry of the Earth was like then . " If a previous civilization had altered the planet 's chemistry -- as humans have done by releasing vast amounts of carbon pollution -- there might be a record . <p> The scientists also considered what other evidence humans might leave behind afterour civilization has ended , like the vast amounts of plastics as well as artificial hormones for agriculture and persistent chemicals , which do not break down in the environment . These might all show up in future sediments , many @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ metals used in electronics . <p> The point of the paper was n't to establish whether the Silurian hypothesis is correct , Frank said . Instead , ? it was " to say here 's the things you 'd want to look for in a much more high-resolution way in order to see whether or not there was ever a civilization before us . " <p> Both Frank and Schmidt are in the strange position of having written a study about a theory neither believes in -- they just say we can not yet rule it out . <p> No one appears to have picked up the call for a deeper investigation in the years since , but some scientists have raised questions . <p> Jan Zalasiewicz , a geologist , paleontologist and emeritus professor at the University of Leicester in the UK , said the Silurian hypothesis is " wonderful and deeply thought-provoking idea . " But Schmidt and Frank underestimated just how much modern humans have transformed the planet , as well as " the effectiveness of the fossilization process and how good it is at preserving a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he said . <p> We ca n't rule out intelligent pre-human societies , " dinosaurs that could sing complex arias , say , or Jurassic ammonites that could compose poetry , " said Zalasiewicz , who co-wrote the 2025 book " Discarded : How Technofossils Will be Our Ultimate Legacy " . But as soon cities are built , metals are smelted , plastics are made and discarded -- these will leave a clear footprint , he said . <p> Zalasiewicz is comfortable ruling out the prior existence of the kind of advanced civilization we live in today -- " energy-guzzling , manipulative , constructional , and producing waste in colossal quantities . " <p> And that 's the beauty of science , Frank said . " You publish a paper , it 's like , ' Woo , this is great , ' and then somebody comes along and says , you 're wrong . " Someone else may find something that points in a different direction , and eventually , as research accumulates , a consensus will be formed . <p> For now , perhaps the most important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ poses about the longevity of advanced technological civilizations like ours . <p> We 're smart enough to develop technology , but we might not be smart enough to figure out how to deal with its climate-shifting consequences , Frank said . " Are we an experiment that the planet has run , which is going to fail ? "
